Philosophy of Law
LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD101 • Legal positivism, natural law, and interpretive adjudication

A city ordinance, duly enacted and published, prohibits sleeping in any public park at any time. Mara, who is unhoused and was turned away from the city's only full shelter, is prosecuted after sleeping on a park bench during a storm. The ordinance is textually clear and no constitutional challenge has yet been adjudicated. As the deciding judge, identify and defend the most persuasive jurisprudential approach to resolving Mara's case.

Answer: The judge should begin with the positive legal materials but should not treat formal enactment as ending the inquiry. The strongest analysis is an interpretive approach that tests the ordinance's text and institutional pedigree against constitutional commitments to dignity, equality, due process, and constrained public power.

Legal Basis: This is a legal-theory exercise, not a request to invent a binding Philippine case. Legal positivism explains why the duly enacted ordinance is presumptively valid; natural-law theory asks whether extreme injustice undermines its claim to legal authority; interpretivism requires reading the legal system as a coherent practice of principle. Article III, Section 1 of the 1987 Constitution supplies genuinely relevant positive-law commitments, but the problem states that no controlling adjudication has resolved the ordinance.

Application: A purely source-based positivist would enforce the clear text unless a superior rule invalidates it. A natural-law account would stress that punishing unavoidable conduct during a storm is morally defective. An interpretive judge should avoid silently rewriting the ordinance, require the prosecution to satisfy all elements, consider any recognized necessity or constitutional defense properly raised, and explain whether enforcing the law against involuntary homelessness is consistent with equal protection and due process. If the record is inadequate for constitutional adjudication, the judge should resolve only what the record permits and identify the institutional limits on judicial lawmaking.

Conclusion: The best answer is a candid, legally constrained interpretive analysis—not automatic enforcement and not free-form moral nullification. Credit depends on accurately distinguishing the theories and defending a resolution consistent with institutional role.

LEB Memorandum Order No. 24, s. 2021, JD101 course framework; 1987 Constitution, Art. III, Sec. 1. LEBMO: https://leb.gov.ph/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/LEBMO-No.-24.pdf; Constitution: https://lawphil.net/consti/cons1987.html

Analytical framework: legal validity, moral legitimacy, and interpretive coherence are distinct inquiries; a judge must state which jurisprudential theory is being used and respect the institutional limits of adjudication.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD103 • Closed-universe source hierarchy and memorandum synthesis

Closed universe: (1) Civil Code Article 2 as amended by Executive Order No. 200; (2) Tañada v. Tuvera, G.R. No. L-63915, December 29, 1986; and (3) an agency circular imposing a new nationwide licensing fee, declaring immediate effectivity, and posted only on the agency website. Prepare a concise predictive memorandum answering whether the circular may presently be enforced against a licensee.

Answer: The better prediction is that the circular is not presently enforceable.

Legal Basis: Executive Order No. 200 requires publication in the Official Gazette or a newspaper of general circulation. Tañada v. Tuvera, G.R. No. L-63915, December 29, 1986, Cruz, J., distinguishes legislative rules that implement law and affect the public from interpretative or purely internal issuances. Rules of general application must be published in full; an immediate-effectivity clause changes timing only after the required publication and cannot dispense with publication. The Court's main resolution declared publication indispensable and ordered publication of covered issuances.

Application: The circular creates a new fee for licensees nationwide and therefore regulates persons outside the agency. It is legislative rather than merely interpretative or internal. Website posting is not one of the publication modes stated in E.O. No. 200. Accordingly, the circular has not acquired binding effect against the licensee.

Conclusion: A court should decline to enforce the fee until proper publication is completed.

Model memorandum structure: Question Presented; Brief Answer; Material Facts; Discussion organized by source hierarchy; Conclusion. Rubric (10 points): accurate issue and prediction—2; correct hierarchy and treatment of E.O. No. 200—2; accurate synthesis of Tañada and its internal/interpretative exception—3; fact-to-rule application—2; concise professional organization and citation—1.

Civil Code, Art. 2, as amended by E.O. No. 200; Tañada v. Tuvera. E.O. No. 200: https://issuances-library.senate.gov.ph/executive-issuance/executive-order-no-200-s-1987; Decision: https://lawphil.net/judjuris/juri1986/dec1986/gr_l-63915_1986.html

In a closed-universe memorandum, the writer must rank binding sources, synthesize the governing rule and its exceptions, distinguish legislative from internal or interpretative issuances, and predict the result without importing outside authorities.

Clinical Legal Education
LEB Model Year 2 • Term 1 • JD105 • CLEP client interviewing, fact development, counseling boundaries, and reflection

CLEP SIMULATION: A tenant arrives at a law-school clinic stating that the landlord changed the locks that morning and kept the tenant's medicines and work equipment inside. The tenant has brought text messages and one unsigned lease draft. Prepare the initial interview plan and the post-interview counseling note that a law student should submit to the supervising lawyer. Do not give the client a final legal opinion.

MODEL WORK PRODUCT:

Interview plan: (1) explain the student's role, supervision, confidentiality limits, and absence of any guarantee of representation; (2) check urgent safety, medical, deadline, and conflict concerns; (3) obtain a chronological narrative before focused questions; (4) clarify possession, rent payments, notices, entry, lock change, property retained, witnesses, communications, and desired outcome; (5) identify and preserve documents, screenshots, receipts, photographs, and witness contacts; (6) ask permission before contacting anyone; and (7) summarize the account back to the client and correct uncertainties.

Counseling note to supervisor: identify verified facts separately from allegations and missing facts; list urgent protective options for the supervisor's assessment; flag that the unsigned lease is not the only possible evidence of the relationship; record the client's objectives; avoid promising a result; and state that no advice will be communicated until reviewed and approved by the supervising lawyer.

Reflection: identify one assumption the interviewer made, one question that may have influenced the answer, and one step needed to make the interview more client-centered.

Performance rubric (10 points): role/confidentiality explanation—2; trauma-informed open-to-focused questioning—2; chronology and factual gaps—2; evidence preservation—1; ethical counseling boundaries and supervisor escalation—2; reflective practice—1.

This simulation does not confer CLE credit, authorize practice, or replace supervised experiential CLEP under Rule 138-A.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD102 • Publication and effectivity of laws

The President signed an executive order imposing compliance duties on all businesses. Copies were circulated to government agencies, but the order was never published in the Official Gazette or in a newspaper of general circulation. An agency immediately penalized Delta Trading under the order. Is the penalty valid?

Answer: No. The penalty is invalid because an unpublished issuance of general application cannot bind the public.

Legal Basis: Article 2 of the Civil Code, as amended by Executive Order No. 200, requires publication before laws and other issuances of general application take effect. Tañada v. Tuvera held that publication is indispensable, although interpretative and purely internal issuances are excluded.

Application: The order imposes duties on all businesses and is neither merely interpretative nor internal. Circulation only among agencies is not the publication required by Article 2. It therefore had not become effective when Delta was penalized.

Conclusion: Delta's penalty must be set aside for lack of an effective, published legal basis.

Civil Code, Article 2, as amended by Executive Order No. 200; publication in the Official Gazette or a newspaper of general circulation is a condition for effectivity of issuances of general application.

Laws and presidential or administrative issuances of general application must be published before they may bind the public; only interpretative regulations and internal directives that do not affect the public are exempt.

Lorenzo M. Tañada, Abraham F. Sarmiento, and Movement of Attorneys for Brotherhood, Integrity and Nationalism, Inc. (MABINI) v. Hon. Juan C. Tuvera, Hon. Joaquin Venus, Melquiades P. de la Cruz, et al.
G.R. No. L-63915, December 29, 1986 (Cruz, J., En Banc)

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD102 • Constitutional title-of-bill requirement

Republic Act No. 7354 is entitled the Philippine Postal Service Act of 1992. Section 35 withdrew most statutory franking privileges. A judge attacks Section 35 solely because the title does not separately mention the withdrawal of franking privileges. Does that title-clause challenge succeed?

Answer: No. The title-clause challenge does not succeed.

Legal Basis: Article VI, Section 26(1) of the Constitution requires every bill to embrace only one subject expressed in its title. Philippine Judges Association v. Prado held that the general title of Republic Act No. 7354 was broad enough to cover the withdrawal of franking privileges as part of reorganizing the postal service.

Application: The withdrawal directly concerns postal operations and revenues and is germane to the statute's expressed subject. The Constitution does not require the title to catalogue every detail. Although the Court invalidated the particular withdrawal on equal-protection grounds, it rejected the title-clause objection.

Conclusion: The challenge based solely on the title fails.
1987 Constitution, Article VI, Section 26(1); Republic Act No. 7354, Section 35.
A statute's title need not be an index of all its provisions; it is sufficient if the provision is germane to the single general subject expressed in the title.

The Philippine Judges Association, duly represented by its President Bernardo P. Abesamis, Vice-President Antonio M. Martinez, et al. v. Hon. LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD102 • Self-executing constitutional provisions

At the privatization bidding for a historic government-owned hotel, a Filipino corporation and a foreign corporation submitted equally advantageous offers. The government corporation chose the foreign bidder, arguing that the Filipino-first clause in the Constitution needs an implementing statute. Is that argument correct?

Answer: No. The argument is incorrect.

Legal Basis: Article XII, Section 10, second paragraph of the Constitution commands the State, in grants involving the national economy and patrimony, to give preference to qualified Filipinos. Manila Prince Hotel v. GSIS held this provision to be self-executing and enforceable without further legislation.

Application: The hotel forms part of the national patrimony, and the Filipino corporation is qualified and has matched the foreign bid. The government cannot avoid the constitutional preference by invoking the absence of an implementing law.

Conclusion: The Filipino corporation must be given the constitutional preference.
1987 Constitution, Article XII, Section 10, second paragraph.
A constitutional provision is self-executing when it supplies a sufficient rule by which the right or duty may be enforced; the Filipino-first mandate in Article XII, Section 10 is self-executing.
Manila Prince Hotel v. Government Service Insurance System, Manila Hotel Corporation, Committee on Privatization and Office of the Government Corporate Counsel
G.R. No. 122156, February 3, 1997 (Bellosillo, J., En Banc)

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD102 • Administrative construction cannot amend a statute

A bank uses a regular accounting method that clearly reflects its income. Revenue Regulations No. 4-2011 nevertheless compels it to allocate common costs among its regular banking, foreign-currency deposit, and other income streams through a prescribed gross-income ratio, thereby reducing deductions otherwise allowed by the Tax Code. The BIR made no finding that the bank's method distorted income or facilitated tax evasion. Is the regulation valid?

Answer: No. Revenue Regulations No. 4-2011 is invalid.

Legal Basis: Sections 34(A)(1), 43, 50, and 244 of the National Internal Revenue Code govern business-expense deductions, accounting methods, allocation authority, and revenue regulations. In Department of Finance and Bureau of Internal Revenue v. Asia United Bank, the Court held that RR No. 4-2011 exceeded those provisions: an administrative issuance may implement a statute but may not amend, expand, or override it.

Application: The bank's chosen method clearly reflects income, so Section 43 does not permit the BIR to substitute a mandatory formula without a contrary finding. Section 50 concerns allocation among controlled organizations, trades, or businesses when necessary to prevent tax evasion or clearly reflect income; it does not authorize a uniform allocation among income streams or units within one bank on these facts. The regulation also adds a limitation to deductions granted by Section 34(A)(1).

Conclusion: RR No. 4-2011 is ultra vires and cannot be enforced against the bank.
National Internal Revenue Code, Sections 34(A)(1), 43, 50, and 244; Revenue Regulations No. 4-2011.

A revenue regulation may fill in statutory details but cannot force an accounting allocation without the findings and scope authorized by the Tax Code, or reduce deductions by adding a condition that Congress did not impose.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD102 • Repeal by implication

A government employee incurred medical expenses from injuries suffered in the performance of official duties and invoked Section 699 of the Revised Administrative Code of 1917. The Commission on Audit denied the claim, reasoning that Executive Order No. 292's general repealing clause had erased Section 699. Is the denial proper?

Answer: No. The denial is improper.

Legal Basis: Repeals by implication are disfavored and require clear, irreconcilable inconsistency or a manifest intent to substitute a complete new law. Mecano v. Commission on Audit held that Executive Order No. 292 did not impliedly repeal Section 699 of the old Administrative Code.

Application: The general repealing clause identifies no express repeal of Section 699, and the medical-benefit provision can coexist with the later Code. Mere omission from a general codification is insufficient.

Conclusion: The claim may proceed under Section 699, subject to proof of its factual requisites.
Revised Administrative Code of 1917, Section 699; Executive Order No. 292, general repealing clause.
Implied repeals are not favored; the earlier and later laws must be so irreconcilably inconsistent that both cannot stand, or the later law must plainly cover the whole subject as a substitute.
Antonio A. Mecano v. Commission on Audit
G.R. No. 103982, December 11, 1992 (Campos, Jr., J., En Banc)

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD102 • Expressio unius est exclusio alterius

A subdivision homeowners' association demanded that the developer donate to it a separately titled lot containing the subdivision's water system. It relied on Section 31 of Presidential Decree No. 957, as amended by Presidential Decree No. 1216, which expressly refers to roads, alleys, sidewalks, and playgrounds. Is the developer legally compelled to donate the water-system lot?

Answer: No. The developer is not compelled by that provision to donate the water-system lot.

Legal Basis: Section 31 of Presidential Decree No. 957, as amended by Presidential Decree No. 1216, enumerates roads, alleys, sidewalks, and playgrounds. Daalco Development Corporation v. Palmas Del Mar Homeowners Association applied expressio unius est exclusio alterius and held that the omitted water-system lot was not covered.

Application: The legislature specifically named the common areas subject to the statutory treatment but omitted water-system lots. The court may not add an omitted category, and the facts show no separate donation or animus donandi.

Conclusion: The association cannot compel donation of the lot under Section 31.
Presidential Decree No. 957, Section 31, as amended by Presidential Decree No. 1216.
When a statute expressly enumerates the things on which it operates, courts ordinarily exclude omitted matters and may not supply an additional category absent contrary legislative intent.
Daalco Development Corporation v. Palmas Del Mar Homeowners Association (PDM-HOA), represented by Gil Fernandez, President
G.R. No. 264652, November 4, 2024 (M. Lopez, J., Second Division)

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD102 • Strict construction of penal statutes and sufficiency of information

During a public meeting, police found a kitchen knife inside Berto's backpack. An information charged him under Batas Pambansa Blg. 6 merely for carrying a bladed weapon outside his residence; it did not allege that he carried it in furtherance of, or in connection with, rebellion, insurrection, sedition, coup d'état, conspiracy or proposal to commit those crimes, or any public disorder. Should the information be quashed?

Answer: Yes. The information fails to allege an essential statutory element.

Legal Basis: Section 3 of Batas Pambansa Blg. 6 penalizes carrying specified weapons outside one's residence only when done in furtherance of, or in connection with, the listed crimes or public disorder. People v. Bercadez reaffirmed the strict construction adopted in Purisima v. People.

Application: The pleading alleges possession and location but omits the required nexus to a specified crime or public disorder. A penal statute cannot be enlarged by implication to criminalize mere carrying.

Conclusion: The information should be quashed, without prejudice to refiling a sufficient charge if legally and factually warranted and not barred by prescription.
Batas Pambansa Blg. 6, Section 3.

Penal statutes are strictly construed against the State; an information under B.P. Blg. 6 must allege the statutory connection between carrying the weapon and one of the specified offenses or a public disorder.
People of the Philippines v. Ronnel Buenafe Bercadez
G.R. No. 265123, July 29, 2024 (J. Lopez, J., Second Division)

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD102 • Constitutional exception and ejusdem generis

An executive order allowed Cabinet members to hold, in addition to their Cabinet posts, any other government office designated by the President. The Government argues that Article VII, Section 13 permits this because it says, 'unless otherwise provided in this Constitution.' Does the exception authorize a general presidential designation power?

Answer: No. The exception is not a general authority to appoint Cabinet officials to additional offices.

Legal Basis: Article VII, Section 13 prohibits the President, Vice-President, Cabinet members, and their deputies or assistants from holding another office unless the Constitution itself otherwise provides. Civil Liberties Union v. Executive Secretary construed the exception narrowly and invalidated Executive Order No. 284.

Application: The proposed additional office is not one of the specific ex officio arrangements supplied by the Constitution. The quoted exception refers to constitutional provisions, not to an unrestricted executive designation.

Conclusion: The designation is prohibited and the executive order cannot validate it.
1987 Constitution, Article VII, Section 13; Executive Order No. 284.

A constitutional exception to the ban on multiple offices is strictly confined to additional functions expressly supplied by the Constitution or performed ex officio as required by the official's primary duties.
Civil Liberties Union v. The Executive Secretary; Anti-Graft League of the Philippines, Inc. and Crispin T. Reyes v. Philip Ella C. Juico, as Secretary of Agrarian Reform, et al.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD102 • Plain meaning in local recall limitations

A recall election against a municipal mayor was scheduled more than one year after the mayor assumed office and more than one year before the next regular local election. The mayor argues that a Sangguniang Kabataan election held in between is itself a “regular local election” within the one-year prohibition in Section 74(b) of the Local Government Code. Is the mayor correct?

Answer: No. An Sangguniang Kabataan election is not the 'regular local election' contemplated by Section 74(b).

Legal Basis: Section 74(b) of Republic Act No. 7160 bars recall within one year from assumption of office or within one year immediately preceding a regular local election. Paras v. Commission on Elections held that the phrase refers to the regular election for the office sought to be recalled, not an SK election.

Application: The SK election does not elect the municipal mayor and does not trigger the statutory waiting period. On the stated dates, neither express prohibition applies.

Conclusion: The intervening SK election does not bar the recall.
Republic Act No. 7160, Section 74(b).
The phrase 'regular local election' in the recall limitation refers to the regular election for the local office concerned; it does not include a Sangguniang Kabataan election.
Danilo E. Paras v. Commission on Elections
G.R. No. 123169, November 4, 1996 (Francisco, J., En Banc)

Statutory Construction
LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD102 • Prospective application of a new judicial doctrine

Police secured a search warrant for pirated videotapes in 1986 by presenting sworn depositions to the judge and reasonably following the then-prevailing interpretation of the examination requirement. Years later, a new decision imposed a stricter procedure. Must the warrant automatically be voided by retroactive application of the new rule?

Answer: No. A genuinely new procedural doctrine should not automatically be applied retroactively to officers who relied in good faith on the prevailing rule.

Legal Basis: Columbia Pictures, Inc. v. Court of Appeals held that the stricter doctrine later announced in 20th Century Fox Film Corporation v. Court of Appeals could not invalidate an earlier warrant obtained in good-faith reliance on the law as then understood.

Application: The officers presented sworn supporting evidence and complied with the interpretation controlling when the warrant issued. Retroactive application would penalize reliance on the judicial rule then in force.

Conclusion: The warrant is not invalid solely because of the later, stricter doctrine.
Rule 126 search-warrant requirements; doctrine on prospective application of a newly announced judicial rule.
A novel judicial doctrine may be applied prospectively where retroactive application would unfairly prejudice parties who relied in good faith on the prior controlling interpretation.

Basic Legal and Judicial Ethics
LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD201 • Conflict of interest between present and former clients

Attorney Rina represented Solis Corp. in negotiating a supply agreement and learned its confidential pricing model. Six months after the engagement ended, a competitor asks her to sue to rescind that same agreement and to use what she knows about Solis’s pricing. Solis has given no written consent. May Rina accept?

Answer: No. Rina may not accept the materially adverse engagement without Solis Corp.’s written informed consent, and she may not use or reveal Solis’s confidential pricing information except as the CPRA permits.

Legal Basis: Canon III, Sections 18(a) and 18(b) of the CPRA preserve a former client’s confidences and prohibit their unauthorized use. Section 18(c) bars representation in the same or a related matter materially adverse to a former client unless that former client gives written informed consent. VERA LAW (Del Rosario Bagamasbad & Raboca) v. Atty. Editha R. Hechanova applied these current provisions; Benedicto Hornilla and Atty. Federico D. Ricafort v. Atty. Ernesto S. Salunat likewise explains the substantial-relation and confidentiality concerns in successive representation.

Application: The proposed suit attacks the very agreement Rina negotiated for Solis. Solis’s pricing model is confidential information material to that suit, the interests are directly adverse, and Solis has not given written informed consent.

Conclusion: Rina must decline the competitor’s engagement and must continue to protect Solis’s confidences.

CPRA, Canon III, Sections 18(a)-(c) (former-client confidences and materially adverse representation); Section 13 (conflicting interests). Official CPRA: https://sc.judiciary.gov.ph/22-09-01-sc-code-of-professional-responsibility-and-accountability/
VERA LAW official decision: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/69853
Hornilla official decision: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/48485

A lawyer may not represent a new client against a former client in the same or a related matter when the new client’s interests are materially adverse, absent the former client’s written informed consent; former-client confidences also may not be used or revealed without authority.
VERA LAW (Del Rosario Bagamasbad & Raboca) v. Atty. Editha R. Hechanova; Benedicto Hornilla and Atty. Federico D. Ricafort v. Atty. Ernesto S. Salunat

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD201 • Attorney-client privilege and confidentiality

During a private consultation, Noel tells Atty. Pia that he may file a civil action and gives her embarrassing financial records so she can advise him. Noel pays no fee and never retains her. Pia later represents the proposed defendant and publicly reveals the records. Is Pia’s conduct proper?

Answer: No. The duty to protect a prospective client’s private confidences does not depend on payment of a fee or a completed retainer.

Legal Basis: Canon III, Section 17(b) of the CPRA requires a lawyer to maintain the private confidences of a prospective client even if no engagement follows and forbids their use for the lawyer or a current client. Rosa F. Mercado v. Atty. Julito D. Vitriolo recognizes that payment is not indispensable to a confidential consultation for legal advice, although the complaint there was dismissed because the complainant failed to identify and prove the alleged confidential communication.

Application: Unlike Mercado’s evidentiary failure, the facts identify the records, establish that Noel privately supplied them for legal advice, and establish Pia’s later disclosure for an adverse client. No CPRA exception or informed consent appears.

Conclusion: Pia’s disclosure is improper, and she may not use the information or continue an adverse representation that the CPRA does not permit.

CPRA, Canon III, Section 17(b) (prospective-client confidences). Official CPRA: https://sc.judiciary.gov.ph/22-09-01-sc-code-of-professional-responsibility-and-accountability/
Mercado official decision: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/42879

A lawyer must protect a prospective client’s private confidences even when no fee is paid and no engagement follows; the claimant must still prove that the information was confidentially communicated for legal advice.

A.C. No. 5108, May 26, 2005 — Puno, J.; complaint dismissed because the alleged confidential communication was not sufficiently identified and proved.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD201 • Client funds and accounting

A client gives Atty. Berto ₱80,000 solely for filing fees. Berto uses the money for office rent, delays filing the action, and returns the amount only after an administrative complaint is filed. Does repayment erase the ethical breach?

Answer: No. The unauthorized use and failure to account were completed breaches; belated repayment does not erase them.

Legal Basis: Canon III, Section 49 of the CPRA requires immediate accounting and limits use of entrusted funds to the declared purpose, with prompt return of unused funds. Section 50 requires client funds to be kept separate from the lawyer’s own funds. Dominador P. Burbe v. Atty. Alberto C. Magulta held that using money entrusted for filing fees and failing to institute the action violated the lawyer’s duties; later reimbursement did not exculpate the lawyer.

Application: Berto received the ₱80,000 for one limited purpose but diverted it to rent, failed to file timely, and accounted only after a complaint. Restitution may be considered under the current penalty framework, but it does not undo the misuse and neglect.

Conclusion: Berto is administratively liable; any sanction must be fixed under the CPRA’s current accountability provisions.

CPRA, Canon III, Sections 49-50 (accounting, use, segregation, and return of client funds). Official CPRA: https://sc.judiciary.gov.ph/22-09-01-sc-code-of-professional-responsibility-and-accountability/
Burbe official decision: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/51195
Funds entrusted for a declared client purpose must be segregated, used only for that purpose, promptly accounted for, and returned when unused; restitution after complaint is not exculpatory.
Dominador P. Burbe v. Atty. Alberto C. Magulta

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD201 • Diligence and abandonment

Atty. Celia accepts an appeal, receives the record, and repeatedly assures her client that the brief was filed. She actually misses the critical appellate deadline and ignores court notices because the client still owes part of the agreed fee. Is nonpayment a defense?

Answer: No. Unpaid fees do not excuse neglect, abandonment, or a false report to the client.

Legal Basis: Canon IV, Sections 1, 3, 4, and 6 of the CPRA require competence, seasonable diligence, avoidance of delay, and regular client updates. Canon III, Section 53(e) allows deliberate nonpayment to constitute good cause for termination, but withdrawal requires written notice and protection against foreseeable prejudice. Veronica S. Santiago, Benjamin Q. Hontiveros, Ma. Socorro F. Manas, and Trinidad Nordista v. Atty. Amado R. Fojas holds that counsel who accepts an engagement must protect the client’s interests with diligence.

Application: Celia accepted the appeal, missed a critical deadline, ignored notices, and falsely claimed compliance. If deliberate nonpayment justified ending the engagement, she still had to follow Section 53 rather than abandon the matter.

Conclusion: Nonpayment is no defense to Celia’s neglect and dishonesty; she is administratively liable under the current CPRA.

CPRA, Canon IV, Sections 1, 3, 4, and 6 (competence, diligence, avoidance of delay, client updates); Canon III, Section 53(e) (termination for deliberate nonpayment with written notice). Official CPRA: https://sc.judiciary.gov.ph/22-09-01-sc-code-of-professional-responsibility-and-accountability/
Santiago decision: https://lawphil.net/judjuris/juri1995/sep1995/ac_4103_1995.html
A lawyer who has accepted an engagement must act diligently and communicate truthfully; deliberate nonpayment may support proper termination, but never abandonment that prejudices the client.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD201 • Candor toward the tribunal

Before the hearing, counsel learns that a material allegation in her verified motion is false. Instead of correcting it, she repeats the allegation orally because it improves her client’s chance of obtaining an injunction. Has she violated professional duty?

Answer: Yes. Advocacy does not permit a lawyer knowingly to maintain or repeat a material falsehood before a tribunal.

Legal Basis: Canon II, Sections 1 and 8 of the CPRA prohibit deceit and misleading a court through a misrepresentation or assertion of an unproved fact. Section 11 prohibits false statements and requires prompt correction of a material false statement in a pleading or other submission. Canon III, Section 2 confines zealous advocacy within the law and the CPRA. Walter T. Young v. Ceasar G. Batuegas, Miguelito Nazareno V. Llantino, and Franklin Q. Susa disciplined the lawyers responsible for a pleading containing a material falsehood about its filing.

Application: Counsel knows the allegation is false but deliberately repeats it to secure judicial relief. That conduct misleads the tribunal, violates candor, and triggers the duty to correct the record.

Conclusion: Counsel must promptly correct the falsehood and may be held administratively liable under the CPRA’s current sanction framework.

CPRA, Canon II, Sections 1, 8, and 11 (honesty, candor, and correction of false statements); Canon III, Section 2 (zeal within legal and ethical bounds). Official CPRA: https://sc.judiciary.gov.ph/22-09-01-sc-code-of-professional-responsibility-and-accountability/
Young official decision: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/47320
A lawyer must not knowingly make, adopt, or perpetuate a material false statement before a tribunal and must promptly correct a material misrepresentation previously made.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD201 • Social-media confidentiality

A lawyer posts on a public social-media account that a named former client has a sexually transmitted infection, information learned solely during representation. The lawyer says the case is over and the post was made in a personal capacity. Is the post permissible?

Answer: No. Professional confidentiality survives the engagement and applies to a lawyer’s online conduct, including a personal account.

Legal Basis: Canon II, Sections 40 and 41 of the CPRA prohibit unauthorized online disclosure of confidential information and require safeguards for client confidences in social media. Canon III, Sections 18(a) and 27 preserve former-client confidentiality, subject only to the limited exceptions in Section 28. In Atty. Rogelio S. Constantino v. Atty. Nemesio A. Aransazo, Jr., the Court held that a professional relationship begins when a person consults a lawyer for legal advice and disciplined a lawyer who disclosed a former client’s confidential information in a sworn statement.

Application: The client is identifiable, the diagnosis was learned solely through the engagement, the disclosure is public, and no consent or Section 28 exception is present. Calling the account “personal” does not remove the CPRA’s duties.

Conclusion: The post violates the CPRA. Liability and sanction are determined under the current accountability provisions, not automatically by the penalty imposed under the former code in Constantino.

CPRA, Canon II, Sections 40-41 (online disclosure and social-media safeguards); Canon III, Sections 18(a), 27-28 (former-client confidentiality and exceptions). Official CPRA: https://sc.judiciary.gov.ph/22-09-01-sc-code-of-professional-responsibility-and-accountability/
Constantino official decision: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/67199

A lawyer may not use social media, including a personal account, to disclose an identifiable current or former client’s confidential information; the duty survives termination unless a defined CPRA exception applies.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD201 • Fee sharing with a nonlawyer

A claims agent refers injury clients to Atty. Leo. They agree that the agent will receive thirty percent of every attorney’s fee collected, although the agent is not a lawyer and performs no legal work. Is the arrangement valid?

Answer: No. A lawyer may not share legal fees with an unlicensed person merely for procuring clients.

Legal Basis: Canon II, Section 17 of the CPRA prohibits direct or indirect solicitation of legal business. Canon III, Section 43 prohibits direct or indirect sharing of legal fees with an unlicensed person or organization outside the rule’s limited exceptions. Tan Tek Beng v. Timoteo A. David rejected a fee-sharing and referral arrangement with a nonlawyer as malpractice.

Application: The agent’s thirty-percent share is compensation for referrals, not authorized legal work, and no Section 43 exception applies. The arrangement encourages solicitation and risks nonlawyer influence over professional judgment.

Conclusion: The fee-sharing agreement is prohibited, and Leo must reject it and prevent solicitation undertaken on his behalf.

CPRA, Canon II, Section 17 (direct or indirect solicitation); Canon III, Section 43 (sharing legal fees with an unlicensed person or organization). Official CPRA: https://sc.judiciary.gov.ph/22-09-01-sc-code-of-professional-responsibility-and-accountability/

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD201 • Meaning of practice of law

Article IX-C, Section 1(1) of the Constitution requires that the COMELEC Chair be a member of the Philippine Bar engaged in the practice of law for at least ten years. Nominee N spent twelve years in a government regulatory office drafting regulations and contracts, rendering legal opinions, and representing the agency in administrative proceedings, but appeared in court only twice. Does N satisfy the ten-year practice requirement?

Answer: Yes, provided N’s work throughout the period genuinely required the application of law, legal principles, training, and professional judgment.

Legal Basis: Article IX-C, Section 1(1) of the 1987 Constitution sets the ten-year practice requirement for the COMELEC Chair. Canon III, Section 1 of the CPRA defines practice of law as legal service or the application of law and legal judgment in or out of court, including qualifying public or private employment. Renato L. Cayetano v. Christian Monsod, Hon. Jovito R. Salonga, Commission on Appointments, and Hon. Guillermo Carague, in his capacity as Secretary of Budget and Management held that practice is not confined to courtroom advocacy and upheld Monsod’s qualification.

Application: Drafting regulations and contracts, rendering legal opinions, and representing an agency in administrative proceedings characteristically apply legal knowledge and judgment. Only two court appearances do not negate twelve years of genuine legal work.

Conclusion: N satisfies the requirement if the stated functions and duration are proved; courtroom frequency is not determinative.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD201 • Judicial appearance of impropriety

While a land case is pending, the judge privately attends the plaintiff’s birthday dinner, sits at the family table, and later posts a photograph captioned “with my closest friends.” No discussion of the case is proved. Must the judge consider inhibition?

Answer: The judge must disclose the relationship and seriously consider voluntary inhibition, but friendship alone is not an automatic ground for mandatory inhibition.

Legal Basis: Canon III, Sections 2 to 4, 6, and 9 of the 2025 Code of Judicial Conduct and Accountability require actual and apparent impartiality and avoidance of interactions that undermine public confidence. Section 11 states the mandatory grounds; Sections 12 and 13 govern voluntary inhibition, disclosure, and a stated reason. Canon IV, Section 7 requires avoidance of impropriety and its appearance. Re: Letter of Presiding Justice Conrado M. Vasquez, Jr. on CA-G.R. SP No. 103692 [Antonio Rosete, et al. v. Securities and Exchange Commission, et al.] underscores that judges must avoid conduct reasonably creating an appearance of partiality.

Application: The pending litigant’s place at a private family celebration and the judge’s public description of the litigant as a “closest friend” would cause a reasonable informed observer to question neutrality. If no Section 11 ground exists, inhibition is not automatically mandatory; the judge must disclose the facts and apply Section 12. Continued handling after disclosure requires the parties’ agreement embodied in an order.

Conclusion: Disclosure and a serious voluntary-inhibition assessment are required; the facts stated do not by themselves establish automatic mandatory disqualification.

2025 Code of Judicial Conduct and Accountability, Canon III, Sections 2-4, 6, 9, and 11-13; Canon IV, Section 7. Official CJCA: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/11/100836

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD201 • Judicial competence and conduct outside court

A trial judge repeatedly invokes private supernatural consultations to explain rulings, announces those consultations from the bench, and allows them to disrupt hearings. He insists that private belief is beyond discipline. Is he correct?

Answer: No. Private belief is protected, but official conduct that lets belief dictate adjudication or disrupt court work may be disciplined.

Legal Basis: Canon IV, Section 12 of the 2025 Code of Judicial Conduct and Accountability protects freedom of religion and belief only insofar as its exercise remains compatible with judicial dignity, impartiality, and independence. Section 13(c) requires decisions to rest strictly on law and evidence, and Section 13(d) bars imposing religious practices on court users. Canon VI, Sections 1 and 3 require competence, diligence, and personally written decisions based on facts, law, rules, and jurisprudence. Office of the Court Administrator v. Judge Florentino V. Floro, Jr.; Re: Resolution Dated 11 May 1999 of Judge Florentino V. Floro, Jr.; and Luz Arriego v. Judge Florentino V. Floro, Jr. distinguished private belief from belief that “spilled over to action” and impaired judicial work.

Application: Discipline would not rest on the judge’s private faith. It may rest on his use of asserted supernatural consultations in official explanations, the displacement of law and evidence, and the disruption of hearings.

Conclusion: The judge may be held administratively accountable for official acts incompatible with adjudication and court administration, not merely for holding a private belief.

Judges retain private beliefs, but those beliefs may not dictate adjudication, replace law and evidence, be imposed on court users, or disrupt judicial work; accountability attaches to incompatible official conduct, not belief alone.
Office of the Court Administrator v. Judge Florentino V. Floro, Jr.; Re: Resolution Dated 11 May 1999 of Judge Florentino V. Floro, Jr.; Luz Arriego v. Judge Florentino V. Floro, Jr.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD401 • Mistake of fact

At midnight, Tomas hears his locked bedroom door being forced open. He repeatedly asks who is there, receives no answer, and is struck when the door breaks inward. Believing a robber is attacking, he uses a knife and kills the intruder, who turns out to be his roommate playing a reckless prank. Tomas was not negligent. Is he criminally liable?

Answer: No. An honest and reasonable mistake of fact, without fault or negligence, negates the criminal intent that would otherwise make the act punishable.

Legal Basis: Revised Penal Code Articles 3 and 11 require the relevant voluntariness and recognize self-defense. United States v. Ah Chong acquitted an accused who acted on reasonable appearances of unlawful aggression without negligence.

Application: Had the circumstances been as Tomas reasonably believed, his defensive act would have been lawful. He demanded identification, faced a forcibly opened door and an apparent blow, and was not careless in forming the belief.

Conclusion: Tomas should be acquitted on mistake of fact in relation to self-defense.

Criminal Law I
LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD401 • Mistake of fact caused by negligence

Police officers are ordered to arrest an armed fugitive. Without confirming identity or making any attempt to arrest, they shoot a sleeping man whom an informer merely points out; the victim is innocent. Can the officers invoke mistake of fact?

Answer: No. The officers cannot invoke mistake of fact to escape liability.

Legal Basis: Articles 3, 11(5), 14(16), 69, and 248 of the Revised Penal Code; People of the Philippines v. Antonio Z. Oanis and Alberto Galanta, G.R. No. 47722, July 27, 1943 (Moran, J.).

Application: Even if the sleeping man had been the fugitive, the arrest order did not authorize his summary killing. He was asleep, unresisting, and could have been identified and arrested without lethal force. The officers intentionally fired without verification, so their error resulted from their own precipitate conduct and does not negate criminal intent. The killing was treacherous and therefore murder. Because they were acting in the performance of a duty but used force that was not a necessary consequence of that duty, the incomplete justifying circumstance may reduce the penalty under Article 69.

Conclusion: The officers are liable for murder, subject to the incomplete fulfillment-of-duty circumstance if proved; mistake of fact does not acquit them.

Mistake of fact excuses only an act that would be lawful if the facts were as believed and when the mistake is without fault or negligence. Police may not kill an unresisting sleeping suspect; an intentional treacherous killing is murder, although incomplete fulfillment of duty may mitigate under Article 69.

Criminal Law I
LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD401 • Impossible crime by physical impossibility

Intent on killing Mina, Carlo fires several shots into the bed where he believes she is sleeping. Mina is abroad and no one is in the room. Carlo has performed every act he planned. Is the offense attempted murder or an impossible crime?

Answer: It is an impossible crime on the stated facts.

Legal Basis: Revised Penal Code Article 4(2), in relation to Article 59, covers acts that would be offenses against persons or property but cannot produce the intended crime because accomplishment is inherently impossible or the means are inadequate or ineffectual. Intod v. Court of Appeals applied this rule when the intended victim was absent from the place fired upon.

Application: Carlo acted with evil intent and completed his planned acts, but killing Mina there was physically impossible because she was absent. The facts do not show an intervening cause after a possible attempt against a present victim.

Conclusion: Carlo is liable for an impossible crime.

Criminal Law I
LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD401 • Attempted versus consummated rape

In 2024, an accused forces a 17-year-old victim to the floor, removes the victim’s clothing, and presses his flaccid penis against the skin above the labia. The victim’s mother intervenes. The evidence proves neither penetration of the vulval cleft nor penile contact with the labia. Is rape consummated?

Answer: No. On the stated facts, rape is not consummated; the offense is attempted rape.

Legal Basis: Articles 6, 266-A(1)(a), and 266-B of the Revised Penal Code, as amended; People of the Philippines v. Efren Agao y Añonuevo, G.R. No. 248049, October 4, 2022 (Caguioa, J., En Banc).

Application: Consummated rape requires the slightest penile penetration into the vulval cleft, understood as penetration of the cleft of the labia majora, by a penis capable of penetration. Mere grazing or surface contact above the labia is insufficient. The forcing, disrobing, and positioning are overt acts directly commencing rape, and the mother’s intervention is an external cause that prevented completion.

Conclusion: The accused is liable for attempted, not consummated, rape.

Under People v. Agao, consummation requires the slightest penetration into the vulval cleft or cleft of the labia majora by a penis capable of penetration; mere surface touching or grazing is not consummated rape. Overt acts stopped by an external cause constitute an attempt.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD401 • No frustrated theft

A shopper conceals a watch in a bag and passes the store’s checkout without paying. A guard stops him before he leaves the building and recovers the watch. Is he guilty only of frustrated theft because he never enjoyed free disposal?

Answer: No. Theft was consummated upon unlawful taking with intent to gain; free disposal is not an additional element.

Legal Basis: Revised Penal Code Articles 6 and 308 define the stages of felonies and theft. Valenzuela v. People held that theft has no frustrated stage because completion occurs when the offender takes personal property without consent and with intent to gain.

Application: The shopper acquired control of the watch and passed the payment point without consent and with intent to gain. Recovery moments later does not undo consummation.

Conclusion: He is liable for consummated theft.

Theft is consummated upon unlawful taking with intent to gain; the ability freely to dispose of the property is not an element.
Aristotel Valenzuela y Natividad v. People of the Philippines and Court of Appeals

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD401 • Unlawful aggression in self-defense

After years of abuse, Bea kills her sleeping husband. At trial she proves battered-woman syndrome but shows no actual or imminent attack when she struck him. Before the statutory defense under R.A. No. 9262 is considered, can she claim complete self-defense under Article 11 of the Revised Penal Code?

Answer: No. Complete self-defense under Article 11 requires unlawful aggression at the time of the defensive act.

Legal Basis: Revised Penal Code Article 11(1) makes unlawful aggression indispensable. People v. Genosa held that battered-woman syndrome did not establish complete self-defense where the husband was not attacking when killed, although the evidence supported mitigating circumstances under the law then applied. R.A. No. 9262 now separately addresses battered-woman syndrome under its own terms.

Application: The long abuse is highly relevant, but the stated facts omit an actual or imminent attack at the decisive moment. Thus Article 11 complete self-defense is unavailable.

Conclusion: Bea cannot be fully justified under Article 11; any defense or mitigation under R.A. No. 9262 must be separately proved.

Unlawful aggression is indispensable to ordinary self-defense; battered-woman syndrome has a separate statutory treatment under R.A. No. 9262.
People of the Philippines v. Marivic Genosa

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD401 • Proximate cause and efficient intervening cause

During a quarrel, Nilo inflicts a small hand wound on Oscar. The wound is medically cleaned and nearly healed. Two weeks later Oscar works barefoot and barehanded in a heavily contaminated field, contracts tetanus from an uncertain source, and dies. Is Nilo automatically liable for homicide?

Answer: No. Liability depends on proof beyond reasonable doubt that Nilo’s wound was the proximate cause of death, without an efficient intervening cause.

Legal Basis: Revised Penal Code Article 4(1) makes a person liable for the natural and logical consequences of a felony. Urbano v. Intermediate Appellate Court reversed a homicide conviction where the evidence did not sufficiently connect the earlier wound to the later tetanus death and an intervening source was plausible.

Application: The wound had been treated and was healing; the later exposure creates a serious causal gap. If medical evidence cannot establish that the original injury caused the fatal infection, criminal causation is not proved.

Conclusion: Nilo cannot be convicted of homicide on causation alone under these facts.

An offender answers for the natural and logical consequences of a felony, but the prosecution must prove proximate causation beyond reasonable doubt; an efficient intervening cause may break the chain.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD401 • Conspiracy proved by coordinated acts

In 2024, ten fraternity officers secretly transport a neophyte to a resort for initiation. Two guard the entrance, several administer blows, and two later carry the unconscious neophyte to a hospital and give a false account. No written agreement is found. May coordinated criminal participation be established?

Answer: Yes, if the prosecution proves each accused’s statutory participation and common design beyond reasonable doubt.

Legal Basis: Section 14 of R.A. No. 11053; Article 8 of the Revised Penal Code; Devie Ann Isaga Fuertes v. Senate of the Philippines, et al., G.R. No. 208162, January 7, 2020 (Leonen, J., En Banc); Dandy L. Dungo and Gregorio A. Sibal, Jr. v. People of the Philippines, G.R. No. 209464, July 1, 2015 (Mendoza, J.).

Application: The blows, guarding, transport, concealment, and coordinated false account are affirmative acts from which a concerted design and individual participation may be inferred; liability is not being based on a written agreement or bare presence alone. Under the current R.A. No. 11053, Section 14 separately defines liability for actual planning or participation and creates a disputable presumption from presence unless the person prevented or promptly reported the hazing without peril. Fuertes upheld the statutory presumption. Dungo illustrates proof by an unbroken chain of coordinated acts, but it construed the former R.A. No. 8049 and is used only to that limited extent.

Conclusion: Criminal participation and conspiracy may be inferred from the coordinated acts, but guilt and the applicable Section 14 category must still be proved individually beyond reasonable doubt.

Current R.A. No. 11053 governs post-2018 hazing. Section 14 defines liability by role and treats presence as prima facie evidence subject to statutory rebuttal; coordinated affirmative acts may independently establish common design and participation beyond reasonable doubt. Dungo is limited to its former-law and circumstantial-evidence context.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD401 • Error in personae and transferred intent

Gardo throws a grenade at the President intending to kill him. The President is unhurt, but a bystander dies. Gardo argues that he never intended to kill the bystander. Is the unintended victim’s death attributable to him?

Answer: Yes. A felon is liable for the natural consequences of the intentional act even when the actual victim differs from the intended victim.

Legal Basis: Revised Penal Code Article 4(1) embodies the rule that criminal liability attaches although the wrongful act differs from that intended. People v. Guillen held the bomber liable for the death caused by the explosive thrown with homicidal intent despite failure to kill the intended target.

Application: Gardo deliberately used a lethal explosive in a crowd. The bystander’s death is a direct consequence of the same felonious act, and error in personae does not erase liability.

Conclusion: He is liable for the resulting death and the legally proper complex or additional offense, as charged and proved.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD401 • Desistance after overt acts

Milo points a loaded pistol at Ana from close range, cocks it, and begins to squeeze the trigger. He then freely changes his mind, lowers the gun, apologizes, and leaves; no person, weapon failure, or outside event prevented the shot. Is he liable for attempted homicide?

Answer: Ordinarily no, because the noncompletion resulted from his own spontaneous desistance, although he remains liable for any other offense already consummated.

Legal Basis: Revised Penal Code Article 6 excludes from an attempted felony a failure to complete the acts of execution caused by the offender’s own spontaneous desistance. Peñaranda v. People applied this rule and explained that voluntary abandonment removes liability for the intended attempted felony but not for physical injuries or another crime already produced.

Application: Milo stopped solely by his own free decision before firing. No external cause thwarted him. Thus an essential element of attempted homicide is absent. Any grave threat, alarm, or firearms offense must be assessed separately under its own elements.

Conclusion: Attempted homicide does not lie on the stated facts, without prejudice to an independently consummated offense.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD301 • Judicial review and constitutional allocation of power

After the House of Representatives proclaimed Arturo elected, his opponent filed an election protest with the constitutionally created Electoral Commission within the period fixed by that Commission but after the deadline earlier stated in a House resolution. Arturo asks the Supreme Court to prohibit the Commission from hearing the protest. Does the Commission have jurisdiction?

Answer: Yes. The Electoral Commission has jurisdiction over the contest.

Legal Basis: Under the constitutional allocation then governing, the Electoral Commission was the sole judge of contests relating to the election, returns, and qualifications of Assembly members. Angara v. Electoral Commission recognized both that exclusive grant and the Supreme Court's authority to determine constitutional boundaries through judicial review.

Application: Once the Constitution vested the contest in the Electoral Commission, the House could not defeat that jurisdiction by its own deadline. The protest was filed within the period validly fixed by the constitutional tribunal.

Conclusion: Prohibition does not lie; the Electoral Commission may hear the protest.
1935 Constitution, Article VI, Section 4; analogous exclusive electoral-tribunal allocation in the 1987 Constitution, Article VI, Section 17.

Jose A. Angara v. The Electoral Commission, Pedro Ynsua, Miguel Castillo, and Dionisio C. Mayor
G.R. No. 45081, July 15, 1936 (Laurel, J., En Banc)

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD301 • Impeachment initiation and the one-year bar

A verified impeachment complaint against an impeachable officer was filed with the House Secretary General and referred to the Committee on Justice. It was later dismissed. Eight months after that initiation, several representatives filed a second impeachment complaint against the same officer. May the House proceed with the second complaint?

Answer: No. The second complaint is constitutionally barred.

Legal Basis: Article XI, Section 3(5) of the Constitution prohibits initiating impeachment proceedings against the same official more than once within one year. Francisco v. House of Representatives held that initiation occurs upon filing of a verified complaint and its referral to the proper House committee.

Application: The first proceeding had been initiated by filing and referral. Its later dismissal did not erase that constitutional event. The second complaint was filed only eight months later.

Conclusion: The House must not proceed with the second complaint until the one-year period has elapsed.
1987 Constitution, Article XI, Section 3(5).
An impeachment proceeding is initiated upon filing of a verified complaint and referral to the House Committee on Justice; another proceeding against the same official within one year is barred.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD301 • Separation of powers and post-enactment legislative intervention

An appropriations law gives every legislator a lump-sum development allocation and permits each legislator, after enactment, to identify the specific projects and beneficiaries to be funded from it. Is that arrangement constitutional?

Answer: No. The post-enactment identification power is unconstitutional.

Legal Basis: Article VI, Sections 1 and 29(1) vest legislative power in Congress and require public funds to be disbursed pursuant to an appropriation made by law. Belgica v. Ochoa invalidated the PDAF system because legislators retained post-enactment authority over project identification and fund release, intruding into execution of the law.

Application: Congress completed the appropriation when the law was enacted. Allowing individual legislators afterward to select projects gives them an implementation role and undermines accountability and separation of powers.

Conclusion: The arrangement is void.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD301 • Savings and transfer of appropriations

Halfway through the fiscal year, the Executive declared unobligated allotments for ongoing projects to be 'savings' and transferred part of them to offices outside the Executive Department for projects not covered by the Executive's own appropriations. Are the declaration and cross-border transfers valid?

Answer: No. Both acts are constitutionally defective on the stated facts.

Legal Basis: Article VI, Section 25(5) allows specified constitutional officers to augment an item in their own appropriations from savings in other items of their respective appropriations. Araullo v. Aquino held that unobligated allotments cannot be treated as savings before the conditions fixed by law are met and that cross-border transfers are prohibited.

Application: Ongoing projects had not produced lawful savings merely because funds were still unobligated midyear. The transfer also crossed from the Executive's appropriations to offices outside that department.

Conclusion: The declaration and transfers are unconstitutional.
1987 Constitution, Article VI, Section 25(5); applicable General Appropriations Act definitions of savings.
Savings must actually exist under law before augmentation, augmentation must support an existing item, and transfers may occur only within the respective constitutional office's own appropriations.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD301 • Emergency powers and the calling-out power

Invoking a presidential proclamation declaring a national emergency, police closed a newspaper office and arrested its editors without warrants even though no statute authorized those acts and no exception to the warrant requirement existed. Were the closure and arrests valid exercises of presidential power?

Answer: No. The proclamation did not create those powers.

Legal Basis: Article VII, Section 18 gives the President calling-out authority, while Article III protects liberty, privacy, speech, and press. David v. Macapagal-Arroyo sustained the President's calling-out power but rejected readings of Proclamation No. 1017 that purported to authorize warrantless arrests, searches, or media takeover beyond the Constitution and existing laws.

Application: Neither a valid warrant exception nor legislation authorized the arrests or closure. A proclamation cannot enlarge police power, suspend civil liberties, or substitute for congressional emergency legislation.

Conclusion: The arrests and closure are unconstitutional.
1987 Constitution, Article III, Sections 2, 3, 4 and 6; Article VII, Section 18; Proclamation No. 1017.
The President's calling-out power does not itself authorize warrantless arrests, searches, seizures, or takeover of private media; government action must rest on the Constitution and existing law.

Constitutional Law I
LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD301 • Legislative inquiry and executive privilege

A Senate committee conducting an inquiry in aid of legislation summoned an executive official to testify about implementation of an agency program. The official refused solely because Executive Order No. 464 required presidential consent; the Executive identified no particular question, document, or recognized privileged communication. Is the refusal justified?

Answer: No. A blanket reliance on Executive Order No. 464 does not justify the refusal.

Legal Basis: Article VI, Section 21 authorizes inquiries in aid of legislation, subject to published rules and respect for rights. Senate of the Philippines v. Ermita invalidated Sections 2(b) and 3 of Executive Order No. 464 insofar as they allowed executive officials to avoid such inquiries without a properly invoked privilege.

Application: This is an inquiry in aid of legislation, not merely the question hour for department heads under Article VI, Section 22. No authorized official made a specific claim explaining how a recognized executive privilege applies.

Conclusion: The official must appear and may resist only particular matters covered by a valid, properly invoked privilege.
1987 Constitution, Article VI, Sections 21 and 22; Executive Order No. 464, Sections 2(b) and 3.
Executive privilege must be invoked with sufficient specificity by proper authority; a blanket requirement of presidential consent cannot defeat Congress's power of inquiry in aid of legislation.

Constitutional Law I
LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD301 • Foreign sovereign immunity

A Philippine contractor sued the United States and its naval officers in a Philippine court for disputes arising from repairs to facilities inside a United States naval base. The repairs were procured to support the foreign state's military mission. The United States did not consent to suit. May the Philippine court exercise jurisdiction?

Answer: No. The suit is barred by foreign sovereign immunity.

Legal Basis: Article II, Section 2 incorporates generally accepted principles of international law into Philippine law. United States of America v. Ruiz applied restrictive sovereign immunity but held that contracts connected with operation of a military base were sovereign, or jure imperii, acts.

Application: The transaction supported a foreign state's military and governmental function rather than an ordinary commercial venture. Without consent, impleading the state and its officers would subject sovereign action to local jurisdiction.

Conclusion: The complaint must be dismissed for lack of jurisdiction over the foreign sovereign.
1987 Constitution, Article II, Section 2; customary international law on restrictive foreign sovereign immunity.

Under restrictive immunity, a foreign state is immune for sovereign or governmental acts (jure imperii), though not necessarily for private or commercial acts (jure gestionis); the nature and purpose of the transaction matter.

Constitutional Law I
LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD301 • Peace agreements and constitutional change

Government peace negotiators initialed an agreement committing the Republic to create a new associative political entity with powers not available under the existing Constitution and to secure whatever constitutional amendments the agreement required. The terms were negotiated without the legally required public consultation. Can the agreement bind the Republic as written?

Answer: No. The agreement cannot bind the Republic as written.

Legal Basis: Constitutional change must follow Article XVII, and executive negotiators remain subject to the Constitution, statutes, and their consultation mandate. Province of North Cotabato v. Government Peace Panel on Ancestral Domain held the MOA-AD unconstitutional because the Executive could not guarantee amendments or assume powers reserved to the sovereign people and constitutional processes.

Application: The panel promised a political structure beyond its present authority and bypassed required consultation. Good-faith peace negotiations do not permit executive agents to pre-commit constitutional outcomes.

Conclusion: The agreement is unconstitutional and may not be signed or implemented in that form.
1987 Constitution, Article XVII; Executive Order No. 3, series of 2001; statutory and constitutional consultation requirements.
The Executive may negotiate peace but cannot guarantee constitutional amendments, create a political entity outside the existing constitutional framework, or evade required public consultation.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD301 • Presidential appointment ban and Supreme Court vacancies

The Chief Justice will compulsorily retire during the period beginning two months before a presidential election and ending when the incumbent President's term expires. Opponents insist that Article VII, Section 15 prevents the incumbent President from filling the vacancy. Under controlling Supreme Court doctrine, does the ban apply to the appointment of the Chief Justice?

Answer: No. Under De Castro v. Judicial and Bar Council, the Article VII, Section 15 appointment ban does not apply to appointments to the Judiciary.

Legal Basis: Article VIII, Section 4(1) commands that a Supreme Court vacancy be filled within ninety days. De Castro harmonized that provision with Article VII, Section 15 and held that the latter's election-period ban concerns executive appointments, not judicial appointments from a JBC shortlist.

Application: The vacancy is in the Supreme Court and the Constitution supplies a mandatory ninety-day filling period. The JBC must complete and submit the shortlist, and the incumbent President may appoint from it notwithstanding the election-period ban.

Conclusion: The appointment is not prohibited by Article VII, Section 15.
1987 Constitution, Article VII, Section 15; Article VIII, Sections 4(1) and 9.

The constitutional election-period ban on presidential appointments does not extend to judicial appointments; Supreme Court vacancies remain subject to the mandatory ninety-day period and the JBC process.

Constitutional Law I
LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD301 • Delegation and contingent legislation

A tax law itself fixes the value-added tax rate at 10 percent but commands the President, upon the Secretary of Finance's recommendation, to raise it to 12 percent once either of two precisely stated fiscal thresholds is reached. The Executive has no discretion to choose another rate or ignore a met threshold. Is this an unconstitutional delegation of legislative power?

Answer: No. This is valid contingent legislation, not an unconstitutional delegation.

Legal Basis: Article VI, Section 1 embodies the nondelegation principle, but Congress may enact a complete law whose operation turns on ascertainment of facts under fixed statutory standards. Abakada Guro Party List v. Ermita sustained Sections 4, 5, and 6 of Republic Act No. 9337 because Congress itself fixed both VAT rates and the objective fiscal triggers.

Application: The Executive neither makes tax policy nor selects the rate. It only ascertains whether a statutory fact has occurred and then performs the consequence Congress already commanded.

Conclusion: The provision is constitutional.
Republic Act No. 9337, Sections 4, 5 and 6; 1987 Constitution, Article VI, Section 1.
Congress may enact a complete law whose operation depends on executive ascertainment of objective facts; fact-finding under fixed standards is not delegation of legislative power.

LEB Model Year 2 • Term 1 • JD501 • Correction of sex entry for intersex person

Alex was registered female at birth but was later medically diagnosed with congenital adrenal hyperplasia and naturally developed predominantly male characteristics. Alex, now an adult, has consistently identified and lived as male and seeks correction of the name and sex entries in the birth certificate. May the court grant the petition?

Answer: Yes, upon competent proof of the intersex condition and the person’s mature choice under the circumstances recognized by jurisprudence.

Legal Basis: Rules 103 and 108 govern changes of name and substantial civil-registry corrections through adversarial proceedings. Republic v. Cagandahan allowed correction for a person with congenital adrenal hyperplasia, recognizing the individual’s natural biological development and adult choice.

Application: Alex’s request is not based solely on preference or cosmetic alteration; it rests on an intersex condition and naturally developed male characteristics. Proper notice, parties, and medical evidence remain required.

Conclusion: The court may grant the requested corrections after a compliant adversarial proceeding.

LEB Model Year 2 • Term 1 • JD501 • Change of sex entry after sex reassignment

Bianca was born biologically male, later underwent sex-reassignment surgery abroad, and petitions under Rule 108 to change the birth-certificate sex entry to female and the first name to a feminine name. No clerical error or intersex condition is alleged. Should the petition be granted under existing Philippine law?

Answer: No. Existing civil-registry statutes do not authorize a change of the recorded sex on that ground alone.

Legal Basis: Republic Act No. 9048, as amended, and Rule 108 govern corrections in the civil registry. Silverio v. Republic held that sex-reassignment surgery does not by itself authorize changing the sex entry fixed by the facts at birth, absent enabling legislation.

Application: Bianca alleges neither an erroneous original entry nor an intersex condition like that in Cagandahan. The requested substantive change cannot be supplied through judicial legislation.

Conclusion: The petition should be denied under current law, without passing on what legislation may later allow.

LEB Model Year 2 • Term 1 • JD501 • Article 26(2) divorce obtained by Filipino spouse

Lara, a Filipino, marries Ken, a Japanese national. While still Filipino, Lara initiates and obtains a valid Japanese divorce that capacitated Ken to remarry. Lara asks a Philippine court to recognize the divorce and declare her capacitated to remarry. Must the foreign spouse have initiated the divorce?

Answer: No. What matters is that a valid foreign divorce was obtained and capacitated the foreign spouse to remarry, not which spouse initiated it.

Legal Basis: Family Code Article 26(2) addresses mixed marriages. Republic v. Manalo held that the provision may apply even when the Filipino spouse initiated the foreign divorce, to avoid the anomalous result of the foreign spouse being free while the Filipino remains bound.

Application: The divorce is valid under Japanese law and restored Ken’s capacity to remarry. Lara must still prove the foreign law and decree as facts in the Philippine proceeding.

Conclusion: Recognition is legally possible despite Lara’s having initiated the divorce.

LEB Model Year 2 • Term 1 • JD501 • Psychological incapacity after Tan-Andal

Before marriage, Paolo repeatedly exploited family members, displayed enduring irresponsibility, and refused any reciprocal obligation. During marriage, the same durable pattern made him incapable—not merely unwilling—of supporting or respecting his spouse and child. Relatives who knew him before marriage testify consistently, but no psychiatrist examined him. Can psychological incapacity be proved?

Answer: Yes. Expert diagnosis or personal psychiatric examination is not indispensable if clear and convincing evidence proves a grave, enduring personality structure that existed at marriage and made compliance with essential marital obligations impossible.

Legal Basis: Family Code Article 36 governs psychological incapacity. Tan-Andal v. Andal clarified that it is a legal, not strictly medical, concept; ordinary witnesses may prove durable dysfunctionality, with gravity, juridical antecedence, and legal incurability understood under the refined standard.

Application: The pre-marriage pattern, continuing dysfunction, and inability to perform Articles 68–71 obligations may satisfy juridical antecedence and gravity. The court must distinguish incapacity from refusal, neglect, or ordinary incompatibility.

Conclusion: The petition may succeed if the total evidence is clear and convincing.

LEB Model Year 2 • Term 1 • JD501 • Article 26 divorce after change of citizenship

Both spouses are Filipino when they marry. Years later, Mira becomes a Canadian citizen and obtains a valid Canadian divorce that allows her to remarry. Her husband Noel remains Filipino. May Noel invoke Article 26(2) in the Philippines?

Answer: Yes. Article 26(2) can apply when one spouse later becomes a foreign citizen and thereafter obtains a valid divorce that capacitates that spouse to remarry.

Legal Basis: Family Code Article 26(2) prevents the absurdity of a Filipino remaining married to a former spouse who is free to remarry under national law. Republic v. Orbecido III identified the requisites for applying the provision to a marriage initially between Filipinos.

Application: Mira was already Canadian when the divorce was obtained, the divorce is valid under Canadian law, and it capacitated her to remarry. Noel must prove those foreign-law facts.

Conclusion: Noel may seek recognition and capacity to remarry under Article 26(2).

LEB Model Year 2 • Term 1 • JD501 • Effect of foreign divorce on alien spouse’s claims

A Filipino wife and her American husband validly divorce in the United States. The husband, capacitated to remarry under his national law, later sues in the Philippines to control the former wife’s business as her husband and to assert spousal management rights. May he do so?

Answer: No. Having obtained a valid divorce binding on him under his national law, the foreign spouse cannot continue asserting rights that depend on the subsistence of the marriage.

Legal Basis: Civil Code Article 15 applies nationality principles to status, while Article 26 of the Family Code addresses mixed marriages. Van Dorn v. Romillo, Jr. held that the alien former husband was estopped from claiming marital rights after a valid foreign divorce.

Application: The American husband is no longer married under the law governing his status and cannot selectively invoke a dissolved marital relationship to control the Filipino former wife’s property or business.

Conclusion: His claims based solely on continuing husband status should be dismissed.

LEB Model Year 2 • Term 1 • JD501 • Proof of foreign divorce and foreign law

Dina presents only an unauthenticated photocopy of a foreign divorce decree and asks a Philippine court to declare her marriage dissolved. She offers no competent proof of the foreign divorce law or its effect on her spouse’s capacity to remarry. Is the showing sufficient?

Answer: No. A foreign judgment and the foreign law under which it was rendered must be alleged and proved as facts in the manner required by the Rules.

Legal Basis: Family Code Article 26(2) is not self-proving as to foreign law. Garcia v. Recio requires competent proof of both the foreign divorce decree and the foreign spouse’s national law showing the decree’s validity and effect.

Application: An unauthenticated photocopy and silence about foreign law do not establish authenticity, validity, or capacity to remarry. Philippine courts do not take judicial notice of foreign law.

Conclusion: The petition must fail without proper proof, without prejudice to a properly supported action.

Family Code, Art. 26(2); Rules of Court, Rules 39 and 132 on foreign judgments and official records. Family Code: https://lawphil.net/executive/execord/eo1987/eo_209_1987.html. Civil Code: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra1949/ra_386_1949.html. Decision: https://lawphil.net/judjuris/juri2001/oct2001/gr_138322_2001.html
Foreign law and a foreign divorce decree are questions of fact that must be competently pleaded and proved; courts do not take judicial notice of them.
Grace J. Garcia, a.k.a. Grace J. Garcia-Recio v. Rederick A. Recio
