LEB Model Year 2 • Term 1 • JD501 • Absence of a marriage ceremony and bigamy

Two Filipinos sign a marriage contract, but no solemnizing officer appears and no marriage ceremony is held. One later marries another person while the first document remains unchallenged. Is the later spouse guilty of bigamy solely because no prior judgment declared the first marriage void?

Answer: No, if the absence of any marriage ceremony is proved.

Legal Basis: Articles 3, 4, and 40 of the Family Code; Article 349 of the Revised Penal Code; Lucio Morigo y Cacho v. People of the Philippines, G.R. No. 145226, February 6, 2004 (Quisumbing, J.); Luisito G. Pulido v. People of the Philippines, G.R. No. 220149, July 27, 2021 (Hernando, J., En Banc).

Application: A signed marriage contract does not substitute for the parties’ appearance before a solemnizing officer and their personal declaration that they take each other as spouses. Without a ceremony, no first marriage came into existence. Morigo therefore found the first element of bigamy absent. Pulido independently confirms the current criminal-law rule that a marriage void ab initio may be raised as a defense to bigamy even without a judicial declaration obtained before the second marriage; Article 40 continues to govern civil capacity to remarry.

Conclusion: Bigamy is not established because the prosecution cannot prove a valid or subsisting first marriage.

No marriage comes into existence without the required ceremony and personal declarations before a solemnizing officer. Under Pulido, a void-ab-initio marriage is a defense to bigamy regardless of when its nullity is judicially declared, while Article 40 remains relevant to civil capacity to remarry.

LEB Model Year 2 • Term 1 • JD501 • Later declaration of nullity and bigamy

A person contracts a second marriage while a first marriage, celebrated with all formal requisites, remains undissolved. During the ensuing bigamy case, a final judgment declares the first marriage void ab initio under Article 36 of the Family Code. May that judgment defeat criminal liability?

Answer: Yes, provided the accused proves that the first marriage was void ab initio; a bare allegation of nullity is not enough.

Legal Basis: Articles 36 and 40 of the Family Code; Article 349 of the Revised Penal Code; Luisito G. Pulido v. People of the Philippines, G.R. No. 220149, July 27, 2021 (Hernando, J., En Banc).

Application: Pulido abandoned the former rule that a judicial declaration of absolute nullity obtained only after the second marriage could not be used as a bigamy defense. A void-ab-initio first marriage is treated as nonexistent for the first element of bigamy, regardless of when the declaration is secured. Article 40 nevertheless remains controlling for civil purposes and requires a final judgment before a party may validly remarry.

Conclusion: The final judgment of nullity may defeat the bigamy charge if its effect and the first marriage’s void character are properly proved.

LEB Model Year 2 • Term 1 • JD501 • Absence versus irregularity of marriage license

A marriage contract recites a marriage-license number, but the local civil registrar issues an authenticated certification after a records search that no license was issued to the spouses and that the cited number belonged to another couple. No suspicious circumstance undermines the certification, and a spouse also testifies that the parties never applied for a license. Is the proof sufficient to overcome the presumption of marriage validity?

Answer: Yes. Taken together, the certification and corroborating evidence are sufficient to prove absence of a valid marriage license.

Legal Basis: Articles 3(2), 4, and 35(3) of the Family Code; Section 28, Rule 132 of the Rules of Court; Lovelle S. Cariaga v. Republic of the Philippines and Henry G. Cariaga, G.R. No. 248643, December 7, 2021 (Caguioa, J.).

Application: A marriage license is a formal requisite, and its absence renders the marriage void unless a statutory exemption applies. Cariaga directs courts to assess a civil registrar’s certification holistically rather than demand talismanic wording. Here, the cited number belonged to another couple, the parties had no license application, the certification is authentic and untainted by suspicion, and the testimony corroborates non-issuance. The presumption of validity is therefore overcome.

Conclusion: The marriage is void ab initio for absence of a valid marriage license.

Proof of no marriage license is assessed holistically. An authentic civil-registrar certification, read with the attendant records and corroborating testimony and unaccompanied by suspicious circumstances, may overcome the presumption of marriage validity.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD101 • Quiz • Law and morality
Distinguish legal validity from moral legitimacy, then explain whether a morally objectionable ordinance can remain legally valid.

Answer: Legal validity and moral legitimacy are related but distinct inquiries. A rule may satisfy the legal system's recognized sources and procedures yet remain open to moral criticism.

Legal Basis: This is a non-case-dependent analytical exercise under the JD101 course description in LEB Memorandum Order No. 24, s. 2021. The Constitution's supremacy and Article III, Section 1 provide positive-law limits against arbitrary deprivation; moral disapproval alone is not a substitute for an identified legal ground.

Application: If an ordinance was validly enacted, a positivist may recognize it as law while still condemning it. A court must invalidate it only through a superior legal norm, such as due process or equal protection, rather than personal moral preference.

Conclusion: The ordinance can be legally valid yet morally objectionable unless a controlling superior norm defeats it.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD102 • Quiz • Self-executing constitutional provisions
Define a self-executing constitutional provision and state the principal test for identifying one.

Answer: A constitutional provision is self-executing when it supplies a sufficient rule by which the right or duty may be enforced without awaiting legislation.

Legal Basis: Courts examine the text, nature, object, and whether enforcement requires policy choices the Constitution left to the legislature. The controlling illustration is Manila Prince Hotel v. Application: A mandatory command identifying the beneficiary and duty may operate directly; a clause expressly calling for legislation usually requires implementation.

Legal Basis: Ultra vires analysis invalidates administrative action only to the extent it exceeds the enabling law, subject to severability. A later code covers government benefits generally but never mentions an older statute granting reimbursement for injuries incurred in official duty; when is implied repeal proper?

Repeal by implication is not favored because legislative intent to repeal should be clear.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD102 • Midterm • Narrow construction of constitutional exceptions
The Constitution prohibits Cabinet members from holding another office 'unless otherwise provided in this Constitution'; may a statute create a broad additional exception?

Answer: No. The exception refers to other constitutional provisions, not an open legislative power to defeat the prohibition.

Legal Basis: Article VII, Section 13 is a direct constitutional limitation. The controlling illustration is Civil Liberties Union v. Application: A statute or executive order cannot convert a narrow textual exception into general permission for multiple offices.

Conclusion: The additional office is prohibited unless the Constitution itself supplies the exception or the function is validly ex officio.

A statute uses an everyday phrase without defining it or assigning a technical sense; what is the starting rule of construction?

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD102 • Final • Prospective application of a new doctrine
A court announces a genuinely new procedural rule after officers completed a search in good-faith reliance on the prior controlling interpretation; must the new rule always invalidate that search?

Answer: No. A novel judicial rule may be applied prospectively when retroactivity would unfairly penalize reasonable reliance on the former doctrine.

Legal Basis: The Court considers the nature of the rule, reliance, and administration of justice. The controlling illustration is Columbia Pictures, Inc., Orion Pictures Corporation, Paramount Pictures Corporation, Twentieth Century Fox Film Corporation, United Artists Corporation, Universal City Studios, Inc., The Walt Disney Company, and Warner Brothers, Inc. v. Court of Appeals, Sunshine Home Video, Inc. and Danilo A. Pelindario, G.R. No. 110318, August 28, 1996 — Regalado, J., En Banc; petition granted and the later, stricter search-warrant doctrine applied prospectively.

Application: The officers followed the controlling procedure existing at the time. The later rule should govern future conduct unless the Court specifies broader reach.

Conclusion: The earlier search is not automatically void under the new rule.
Rules of Criminal Procedure, Rule 126; doctrine on prospective application of a newly announced judicial rule.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD102 • Final • Noscitur a sociis
Define noscitur a sociis and explain when it is properly used.

Answer: An ambiguous word or phrase may be clarified by associated words and surrounding provisions.

Legal Basis: The canon applies only when meaning is doubtful and context supplies a coherent class or subject. The controlling illustration is Coca-Cola Bottlers, Phils., Inc. (CCBPI), Naga Plant v. Application: A broad catch-all in an unfair-competition provision is read alongside passing off, deception, and goodwill, not as a prohibition of every unfair business behavior.

Conclusion: Context narrows the ambiguous phrase to the statutory subject.

Words are known by their associates because statutory language operates as an integrated text.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD102 • Final • Whole-text construction in penal laws
May a prosecutor isolate one broad clause from the rest of a penal statute to establish probable cause?

Answer: No. The clause must be read with definitions, policy, neighboring provisions, and offense elements, with remaining ambiguity resolved strictly.

Legal Basis: Rule 126 requires probable cause for one specific offense that actually exists under law. The controlling illustration is Coca-Cola Bottlers, Phils., Inc. (CCBPI), Naga Plant v. Quintin J. Gomez, a.k.a. 'Kit' Gomez and Danilo E. Galicia, a.k.a. 'Danny Galicia', G.R. No. 154491, November 14, 2008 — Brion, J., Second Division; petition denied and the search warrant declared null because bottle hoarding was outside Section 168.

Application: Isolated language cannot support a warrant when the alleged act falls outside the statute viewed as a whole.

Conclusion: The warrant must be denied or quashed if no statutory offense is alleged.
Republic Act No. 8293, Sections 168 and 170; Rules of Criminal Procedure, Rule 126.
Whole-text construction prevents a general phrase from expanding beyond the scheme Congress enacted.

An act involving marked beverage bottles may violate a specific container statute but not the Intellectual Property Code offense cited in the warrant; can the warrant be upheld by substituting the other law later?

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD102 • Final • Ejusdem generis
A law reserves land for parks, playgrounds, schools, roads, health centers, and 'other similar facilities'; does a community water facility fall within the general phrase?

Answer: Yes. The listed facilities share the class of community-welfare uses, and a water facility is of the same public-serving nature.

Legal Basis: Presidential Decree No. 1216, Section 1 supplies the enumeration and residual phrase. The controlling illustration is Emeteria Liwag v. Happy Glen Loop Homeowners Association, Inc., G.R. No. 189755, July 4, 2012 — Sereno, J., Second Division; petition denied and the water-facility lot held within 'other similar facilities and amenities' under ejusdem generis.

Application: Reliable water is a basic facility serving the residential community, not a private commercial use.

Conclusion: The water-facility site falls within the residual class.
Presidential Decree No. 1216, Section 1; Civil Code, Articles 613, 614, and 620.
Ejusdem generis includes unlisted matters akin to the discernible class formed by the specific terms.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD102 • Final • Requirements of ejusdem generis
Enumerate and discuss the conditions that ordinarily justify use of ejusdem generis.

Answer: There should be specific terms forming a discernible class, an associated general term, no contrary intent, and an unlisted matter fairly belonging to that class.

Legal Basis: The canon serves the whole text rather than replacing it. The controlling illustration is Emeteria Liwag v. Happy Glen Loop Homeowners Association, Inc., G.R. Application: If examples are unrelated and form no class, or the statute says the list is unrestricted, narrowing the general term would be improper.

Conclusion: Apply the canon only when text and structure support a common class.

Ejusdem generis gives effect to specific and general words by using examples to define the residual category.

A statute lists unrelated examples—cash, wetlands, radio frequencies, and court records—then says 'and all other assets of every kind'; should the catch-all be narrowed to one class?

Conclusion: The broad catch-all should receive its ordinary comprehensive meaning.

Basic Legal and Judicial Ethics
LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD201 • Quiz • Former-client conflict in the same matter
A lawyer who drafted a seller's disputed contract is later asked by the buyer to rescind that same contract against the former client; may the lawyer accept without consent?

Answer: No. The new matter is the same transaction and the new client's interests are materially adverse to the former client's interests.

Legal Basis: Section 18(c) requires the former client's written informed consent, while Sections 18(a) and (b) preserve confidences and restrict their use. The directly relevant authority is VERA LAW (Del Rosario Bagamasbad & Raboca) v. Atty. Editha R. Hechanova; Benedicto Hornilla and Atty. Federico D. Ricafort v. Atty. Ernesto S. Salunat, A.C. No. 13986 (Formerly CBD Case No. 12-3681), February 26, 2025 — Gaerlan, J.; conflict violations sustained and suspension imposed; A.C. No. 5804, July 1, 2003 — Ynares-Santiago, J.; respondent admonished.

Application: The lawyer would attack the very instrument previously prepared for the seller and risks using knowledge gained in that engagement.

Conclusion: The lawyer must decline unless the former client gives valid written informed consent after full disclosure.
CPRA, Canon III, Sections 13 and 18(a)-(c).
Loyalty and confidentiality survive termination and bar materially adverse representation in the same or a related matter without the prescribed consent.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD201 • Quiz • Use of former-client information
After an engagement ends, counsel uses the former client's confidential settlement ceiling to negotiate for a new client in an unrelated lawsuit against that former client; is the use proper?

Answer: No. A lawyer may not use information relating to former representation to the former client's disadvantage unless the CPRA or law permits it or the information is generally known.

Legal Basis: Section 18(b) separately prohibits use even when the new lawsuit is not substantially related. The directly relevant authority is VERA LAW (Del Rosario Bagamasbad & Raboca) v. Atty. Editha R. Hechanova; Benedicto Hornilla and Atty. Federico D. Ricafort v. Atty. Ernesto S. Salunat, A.C. No. 5804, July 1, 2003 — Ynares-Santiago, J.; respondent admonished.

Application: The confidential ceiling materially strengthens the new client's bargaining position and was learned through the prior professional relationship.

Conclusion: The lawyer must not use the information and should withdraw if competent representation cannot proceed without it.
CPRA, Canon III, Sections 13 and 18(a)-(b).
The former-client rule protects information from use as well as disclosure.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD201 • Quiz • Generally known information and former clients
A former client objects when the lawyer cites a fact contained in a widely published final Supreme Court decision; does former-client confidentiality automatically bar all use of that fact?

Answer: Not automatically. Section 18 recognizes that information which has become generally known is treated differently, although other duties and conflicts may still apply.

Legal Basis: The lawyer must distinguish information genuinely public and generally known from confidential context or strategy not revealed by the decision. The directly relevant authority is VERA LAW (Del Rosario Bagamasbad & Raboca) v. Atty. Editha R. Hechanova; Benedicto Hornilla and Atty. Federico D. Ricafort v. Atty. Ernesto S. Salunat, A.C. No. 5804, July 1, 2003 — Ynares-Santiago, J.; respondent admonished.

Application: The published holding may be cited, but unpublished client communications and litigation strategy remain protected.

Conclusion: Use of the public decision alone is not a confidentiality breach on these facts.
CPRA, Canon III, Sections 13 and 18(a).
A public record does not necessarily disclose every protected client confidence; the exception is limited to what is actually generally known.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD201 • Quiz • Written informed consent to conflict
Both sides orally tell a former lawyer over dinner that they do not mind the lawyer's adverse appearance in a related case; is that oral assent sufficient?

Answer: No. The CPRA requires written informed consent after disclosure of the material risks and reasonably available alternatives.

Legal Basis: Sections 13 and 18(c) make form and informed disclosure substantive safeguards, not technicalities. The directly relevant authority is VERA LAW (Del Rosario Bagamasbad & Raboca) v. Atty. Editha R. Hechanova; Benedicto Hornilla and Atty. Federico D. Ricafort v. Atty. Ernesto S. Salunat, A.C. No. 5804, July 1, 2003 — Ynares-Santiago, J.; respondent admonished.

Application: A casual oral statement does not create a reliable record that the former client understood how loyalty, confidentiality, and litigation position may be affected.

Conclusion: The lawyer may not accept on the strength of oral assent.
CPRA, Canon III, Sections 13 and 18(c).
Consent to conflict must be informed, voluntary, and in the form expressly required by the CPRA.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD201 • Quiz • Simultaneous representation of opposing interests
One lawyer represents a lender in collecting a loan while simultaneously advising the borrower how to defeat that same collection; may both clients consent verbally?

Answer: No. The lawyer is required to fight for a claim for one client and oppose it for the other, creating a direct conflict; only written informed consent after full disclosure can satisfy Section 13, and representation may still be untenable if competent loyalty cannot be maintained.

Legal Basis: Section 14(b) also bars use of one current client's confidential information without written informed consent. The directly relevant authority is VERA LAW (Del Rosario Bagamasbad & Raboca) v. Atty. Editha R. Hechanova; Benedicto Hornilla and Atty. Federico D. Ricafort v. Atty. Ernesto S. Salunat, A.C. No. 13986 (Formerly CBD Case No. 12-3681), February 26, 2025 — Gaerlan, J.; conflict violations sustained and suspension imposed; A.C. No. 5804, July 1, 2003 — Ynares-Santiago, J.; respondent admonished.

Application: The duties are directly contradictory in the same controversy, making effective representation highly doubtful.

Conclusion: The lawyer should not undertake both sides of the dispute.
CPRA, Canon III, Sections 13 and 14(b).
Direct adversity in the same matter presents the core conflict-of-interest test and ordinarily requires refusal, not divided loyalty.
VERA LAW (Del Rosario Bagamasbad & Raboca) v. Atty. Editha R. Hechanova; Benedicto Hornilla and Atty. Federico D. Ricafort v. Atty. Ernesto S. Salunat

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD201 • Quiz • Prospective-client confidentiality without engagement
A person privately consults a lawyer, discloses an unfiled defense, pays no fee, and later hires someone else; may the consulted lawyer reveal the defense to the opponent?

Answer: No. The duty to preserve a prospective client's private confidences exists even when no engagement or fee follows.

Legal Basis: Section 17(b) protects information disclosed in a consultation for possible legal service. The directly relevant authority is Rosa F. Mercado v. Atty. Julito D. Vitriolo, A.C. No. 5108, May 26, 2005 — Puno, J.; complaint dismissed because the alleged confidential communication was not sufficiently identified and proved.

Application: The defense was communicated privately for legal advice and is not generally known.

Conclusion: The consulted lawyer must keep it confidential and may not use it for the opponent.
CPRA, Canon III, Section 17(a)-(b).
Prospective-client protection prevents consultations from becoming traps and does not depend on payment.
Rosa F. Mercado v. Atty. Julito D. Vitriolo
A.C. No. 5108, May 26, 2005 — Puno, J.; complaint dismissed because the alleged confidential communication was not sufficiently identified and proved.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD201 • Quiz • Early prospective-client conflict check
Before hearing a prospective client's detailed story, what conflict step does the CPRA require at the earliest opportunity?

Answer: The lawyer must ascertain whether a conflict exists between the prospective client and current clients and immediately disclose it if found.

Legal Basis: Section 17(a) is designed to avoid receiving disqualifying information before the lawyer knows the relevant parties and matter. The directly relevant authority is Rosa F. Mercado v. Atty. Julito D. Vitriolo, A.C. No. 5108, May 26, 2005 — Puno, J.; complaint dismissed because the alleged confidential communication was not sufficiently identified and proved.

Application: The lawyer should obtain only the minimum identity and subject information necessary for a conflicts check before inviting detailed confidences.

Conclusion: The detailed consultation should pause if a conflict appears.
CPRA, Canon III, Section 17(a).
Early conflict screening protects current clients, prospective clients, and the lawyer's ability to serve either.
Rosa F. Mercado v. Atty. Julito D. Vitriolo
A.C. No. 5108, May 26, 2005 — Puno, J.; complaint dismissed because the alleged confidential communication was not sufficiently identified and proved.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD201 • Quiz • Client objection after prospective conflict disclosure
A conflict with a current client is found and disclosed, and that current client objects; may the lawyer still accept the prospective engagement because the prospective client consents?

Answer: No. Section 17(a) directs the lawyer not to accept the new engagement when either the prospective or current client objects.

Legal Basis: One party's willingness does not cure the other party's protected interest. The directly relevant authority is Rosa F. Mercado v. Atty. Julito D. Vitriolo, A.C. No. 5108, May 26, 2005 — Puno, J.; complaint dismissed because the alleged confidential communication was not sufficiently identified and proved.

Application: The current client's objection preserves undivided loyalty, and the lawyer already owes the prospective person confidentiality over information received.

Conclusion: The lawyer must decline the new engagement and protect all confidences.
CPRA, Canon III, Section 17(a)-(b).
Conflict consent must satisfy the interests and formal requirements applicable to every person whose loyalty or confidentiality is affected.
Rosa F. Mercado v. Atty. Julito D. Vitriolo
A.C. No. 5108, May 26, 2005 — Puno, J.; complaint dismissed because the alleged confidential communication was not sufficiently identified and proved.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD201 • Quiz • Proof of a prospective confidence
A complainant merely says, 'the lawyer revealed my secrets,' but never identifies the communication, circumstances, or confidential information; is the allegation alone enough for discipline?

Answer: No. The protection is real, but the complainant must prove by substantial evidence that identifiable confidential information was communicated in a prospective professional consultation and was misused or disclosed.

Legal Basis: Mercado dismissed the complaint because the supposed confidential communication was not sufficiently identified and proved. The directly relevant authority is Rosa F. Mercado v. Atty. Julito D. Vitriolo, A.C. No. 5108, May 26, 2005 — Puno, J.; complaint dismissed because the alleged confidential communication was not sufficiently identified and proved.

Application: A conclusion without facts does not allow the tribunal to determine confidentiality, disclosure, or responsibility.

Conclusion: The complaint fails on the stated proof, without denying the governing duty.
CPRA, Canon III, Section 17(b); Rules on Evidence, lawyer-client privilege.
Ethical liability requires substantial evidence; the existence of a rule does not relieve the complainant of proving its factual elements.
Rosa F. Mercado v. Atty. Julito D. Vitriolo
A.C. No. 5108, May 26, 2005 — Puno, J.; complaint dismissed because the alleged confidential communication was not sufficiently identified and proved.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD201 • Quiz • Use of prospective-client information for personal gain
A lawyer declines a startup's consultation but buys shares after learning privately that a confidential merger will be announced; is the trade ethically permissible?

Answer: No. Section 17(b) prohibits using a prospective client's private information to further the lawyer's own interest even if no engagement materializes.

Legal Basis: The duty covers use as well as disclosure and operates independently of securities-law liability. The directly relevant authority is Rosa F. Mercado v. Atty. Julito D. Vitriolo, A.C. No. 5108, May 26, 2005 — Puno, J.; complaint dismissed because the alleged confidential communication was not sufficiently identified and proved.

Application: The lawyer obtained the merger information solely through the prospective professional consultation and trades for personal advantage.

Conclusion: The lawyer must not trade on the information and may face professional and other legal consequences.
CPRA, Canon III, Section 17(b).
A consultation creates a limited fiduciary duty that bars self-interested exploitation of prospective-client confidences.
Rosa F. Mercado v. Atty. Julito D. Vitriolo
A.C. No. 5108, May 26, 2005 — Puno, J.; complaint dismissed because the alleged confidential communication was not sufficiently identified and proved.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD201 • Midterm • Client funds for a declared purpose
A client gives counsel ₱60,000 solely for an appeal bond, but counsel spends it on office rent and misses the bond deadline; is later repayment a complete defense?

Answer: No. Using entrusted money for another purpose is a breach when it occurs, and later repayment does not erase misappropriation or resulting prejudice.

Legal Basis: Sections 49 and 50 require immediate accounting, use only for the declared purpose, segregation, and prompt return of unused funds. The directly relevant authority is Dominador P. Burbe v. Atty. Alberto C. Magulta, A.C. No. 5713, June 10, 2002 — Panganiban, J.; respondent suspended from the practice of law for one year.

Application: Office expenses were not authorized and the missed deadline harmed the client.

Conclusion: The lawyer remains administratively accountable despite repayment.
CPRA, Canon III, Sections 49-50; Canon VI, Section 33(g).
Client funds are held in trust; restitution may affect circumstances but is not exculpation.
Dominador P. Burbe v. Atty. Alberto C. Magulta
A.C. No. 5713, June 10, 2002 — Panganiban, J.; respondent suspended from the practice of law for one year.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD201 • Midterm • Commingling client and personal funds
May a lawyer deposit litigation funds into a personal payroll account if meticulous private notes show the client's balance?

Answer: No. Client money must be kept separate from the lawyer's own funds, subject only to any narrowly permitted amount necessary to maintain the account.

Legal Basis: Section 50 protects traceability, ownership, and availability of entrusted property. The directly relevant authority is Dominador P. Burbe v. Atty. Alberto C. Magulta, A.C. No. 5713, June 10, 2002 — Panganiban, J.; respondent suspended from the practice of law for one year.

Application: Private notes do not prevent creditors, accidental spending, or confusion over ownership in a mixed personal account.

Conclusion: The lawyer must use a proper separate client account or other compliant arrangement.
CPRA, Canon III, Sections 49-50.
Segregation is an independent fiduciary safeguard, not merely an accounting preference.
Dominador P. Burbe v. Atty. Alberto C. Magulta
A.C. No. 5713, June 10, 2002 — Panganiban, J.; respondent suspended from the practice of law for one year.

A client asks for a statement showing filing fees paid and the remaining cash balance, but counsel refuses until the case ends; is refusal proper?

Answer: No. A lawyer must account for client money during the engagement when accounting is due and cannot postpone transparency without lawful reason.

Legal Basis: Section 49 requires immediate accounting and proper use of entrusted funds. The directly relevant authority is Dominador P. Burbe v. Atty. Alberto C. Magulta, A.C. No. 5713, June 10, 2002 — Panganiban, J.; respondent suspended from the practice of law for one year.

Application: Receipts and balances can be reported without compromising litigation strategy, and the client retains an interest in knowing how the money was used.

Conclusion: Counsel should promptly provide an accurate accounting.

Fiduciary custody requires contemporaneous transparency, not an unexplained end-of-case reckoning.

After dismissal of a case, counsel keeps an unused ₱25,000 expense balance because the client has not yet asked for it; may counsel wait indefinitely?

Application: Dismissal ended the anticipated expense need, and no unresolved lawful claim to the amount is stated.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD201 • Midterm • Disputed fees and entrusted expense funds
A lawyer claims an unpaid professional fee and unilaterally takes it from money the client delivered only for sheriff's expenses; is the setoff proper?

Answer: No. Funds entrusted for a specific expense cannot be converted unilaterally into fees; any fee claim must be handled through lawful agreement and remedies, with disputed property protected.

Legal Basis: Sections 49 and 50 require use for the declared purpose and proper accounting. The directly relevant authority is Dominador P. Burbe v. Atty. Alberto C. Magulta, A.C. No. 5713, June 10, 2002 — Panganiban, J.; respondent suspended from the practice of law for one year.

Application: The client did not authorize the fund as a general retainer or fee payment, and the lawyer's self-help defeats the trust purpose.

Conclusion: The lawyer must preserve and account for the expense fund and pursue the fee separately.
CPRA, Canon III, Sections 49-50.
A lawyer's compensation claim does not erase fiduciary duties over property held for a different declared purpose.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD201 • Midterm • Nonpayment and abandonment
A client deliberately stops paying, so counsel silently stops attending hearings without withdrawing or warning the client; is nonpayment a defense?

Answer: No. Deliberate nonpayment may support proper termination, but it does not authorize abandonment that prejudices the client.

Legal Basis: The CPRA requires competence, diligence, communication, and lawful termination with written notice and protective steps. The directly relevant authority is Veronica S. Santiago, Benjamin Q. Hontiveros, Ma. Socorro F. Manas, and Trinidad Nordista v. Atty. Amado R. Fojas, A.C. No. 4103, September 7, 1995 — Davide, Jr., J.; respondent reprimanded and admonished to observe greater care and diligence.

Application: Counsel remained attorney of record and allowed hearings to proceed without representation or leave of court.

Conclusion: Counsel is accountable and should have pursued proper withdrawal.
CPRA, Canon IV, Sections 1, 3, 4, and 6; Canon III, Section 53(e).
A financial dispute never licenses silent abandonment of a professional undertaking.
Veronica S. Santiago, Benjamin Q. Hontiveros, Ma. Socorro F. Manas, and Trinidad Nordista v. Atty. Amado R. Fojas
A.C. No. 4103, September 7, 1995 — Davide, Jr., J.; respondent reprimanded and admonished to observe greater care and diligence.

Conclusion: Counsel must disclose the error, take any lawful remedial step, and face accountability.

Professional diligence includes candid communication about mistakes; concealment is not client protection.

A.C. No. 4103, September 7, 1995 — Davide, Jr., J.; respondent reprimanded and admonished to observe greater care and diligence.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD201 • Midterm • Protective duties upon withdrawal
A court permits counsel to withdraw five days before trial; may counsel keep the file until every disputed fee is paid?

Answer: No. Termination does not permit conduct foreseeably prejudicing the client's case; papers and property needed for representation must be handled under the CPRA and lawful lien rules.

Legal Basis: Withdrawal requires reasonable protective steps, notice, time for new counsel, and delivery of what the client is entitled to receive. The directly relevant authority is Veronica S. No. 4103, September 7, 1995 — Davide, Jr., J.; respondent reprimanded and admonished to observe greater care and diligence.

Application: With trial imminent, withholding the entire working file would materially impair substitute counsel.

Conclusion: Outgoing counsel must facilitate an orderly transition while pursuing any legitimate fee remedy lawfully.
CPRA, Canon III, Section 53; Canon IV, Sections 3-4.
The lawyer's duties at termination protect continuity of representation and the client's legal interests.
Veronica S. Santiago, Benjamin Q. Hontiveros, Ma. Socorro F. Manas, and Trinidad Nordista v. Atty. Amado R. Fojas
A.C. No. 4103, September 7, 1995 — Davide, Jr., J.; respondent reprimanded and admonished to observe greater care and diligence.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD201 • Midterm • Punctuality and repeated delay
A lawyer routinely arrives hours late for hearings because other paying clients are treated as more important; does eventual appearance cure the conduct?

Answer: No. Repeated avoidable lateness violates punctuality and diligence and burdens clients, courts, witnesses, and opposing parties.

Legal Basis: Canon IV requires timely appearances and forbids causing delay in legal matters. The directly relevant authority is Veronica S. Santiago, Benjamin Q. Hontiveros, Ma. Socorro F. Application: Choosing higher-paying matters over scheduled court duties is not an unavoidable emergency and reflects inadequate case management.

Conclusion: The lawyer must correct the practice and may be disciplined.

Diligence is owed to the justice system as well as the client and is not measured only by eventual attendance.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD201 • Midterm • Preparation for trial
Counsel appears for trial without reading the pleadings, knowing the witnesses, or bringing exhibits, then requests postponement; is physical presence sufficient diligence?

Application: The postponement results from counsel's avoidable lack of preparation and risks prejudice and delay.

Conclusion: Counsel has breached professional duties.

Diligence includes substantive readiness to perform the legal task entrusted, not only compliance with the calendar.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD201 • Midterm • Known false allegation before a tribunal
A lawyer knowingly repeats a false material allegation in oral argument because it strengthens a request for injunction; may client zeal justify it?

Answer: No. A lawyer may advance a client's cause only through lawful and ethical means and may not knowingly make or perpetuate a false statement.

Legal Basis: Candor and honesty to the tribunal are independent duties under Canon II. The directly relevant authority is Walter T. Young v. Ceasar G. Batuegas, Miguelito Nazareno V. Llantino, and Franklin Q. Susa, A.C. No. 5379, May 9, 2003 — Ynares-Santiago, J.; Batuegas and Llantino suspended for six months; complaint against Susa dismissed.

Application: The allegation is material, known false, and intentionally used to influence judicial action.

Conclusion: The lawyer must withdraw the statement and correct the record.
CPRA, Canon II, Sections 1, 8, and 11; Canon III, Section 2.
Zeal is bounded by truthfulness and cannot justify deceiving a tribunal.
Walter T. Young v. Ceasar G. Batuegas, Miguelito Nazareno V. Llantino, and Franklin Q. Susa
A.C. No. 5379, May 9, 2003 — Ynares-Santiago, J.; Batuegas and Llantino suspended for six months; complaint against Susa dismissed.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD201 • Midterm • Duty to correct a material misstatement
Counsel later discovers that a material factual statement in a filed motion is false; may counsel remain silent because it was believed true when filed?

Answer: No. Once counsel learns the material statement is false, the duty of candor requires prompt correction through the proper procedure.

Legal Basis: The CPRA prohibits false statements and requires correction of material misrepresentations. The directly relevant authority is Walter T. Young v. Ceasar G. Application: Continued silence would allow the court to act on information counsel now knows is inaccurate.

Conclusion: Counsel should inform the client and promptly correct the record.

Good faith at filing does not justify perpetuating a material falsehood after discovery.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD201 • Midterm • Client demand to present false evidence
A client orders counsel to submit a fabricated receipt and threatens to discharge counsel for refusing; what should counsel do?

Answer: Counsel must refuse to submit the fabricated receipt, advise the client of consequences, and take any further remedial or withdrawal steps required by the CPRA and procedural law.

Legal Basis: No client instruction authorizes false evidence or perversion of legal process. The directly relevant authority is Walter T. Young v. Ceasar G. Batuegas, Miguelito Nazareno V. Conclusion: Counsel must not use the receipt.

Client loyalty exists within the law and the lawyer's duties as an officer of the court.

A lawyer deletes limiting words from a Supreme Court quotation and presents the altered passage as exact; is this merely forceful advocacy?

Answer: No. Deliberately altering a quotation is a false representation to the tribunal and undermines reliable adjudication.

Legal Basis: Candor requires accurate presentation of legal authorities and facts. The directly relevant authority is Walter T. Young v. Ceasar G. Batuegas, Miguelito Nazareno V. Advocacy permits argument about precedent, never falsification of what the precedent says.

Counsel signs a verification claiming personal knowledge although counsel never reviewed the records and simply assumes the allegations are true; is the signature proper?

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD201 • Midterm • Online disclosure of former-client information
After representation ends, a lawyer posts the former client's confidential medical diagnosis to win an online argument; is the post proper?

Answer: No. Confidentiality survives the engagement, and social-media use does not create an exception.

Legal Basis: Canon II, Section 40 prohibits direct or indirect online disclosure of client information except when law or the CPRA permits it. The directly relevant authority is Atty. Rogelio S. Constantino v. Atty. Nemesio A. Aransazo, Jr., A.C. No. 9701, February 10, 2021 — Hernando, J.; respondent suspended from the practice of law for one year.

Application: The diagnosis was learned only through representation, remains private, and is disclosed for personal advantage rather than a recognized exception.

Conclusion: The lawyer must not post it and may be disciplined.
CPRA, Canon II, Sections 40-41; Canon III, Sections 18(a), 27-28.
A lawyer's online persona remains bound by enduring duties of confidentiality.
Atty. Rogelio S. Constantino v. Atty. Nemesio A. Aransazo, Jr.
A.C. No. 9701, February 10, 2021 — Hernando, J.; respondent suspended from the practice of law for one year.

Answer: No. A lawyer may disclose only within a specific exception recognized by the CPRA or law and only to the extent necessary.

Legal Basis: Sections 27 and 28 govern confidentiality and its limited exceptions; Section 40 carries them online. The directly relevant authority is Atty. Rogelio S. Constantino v. Atty. Nemesio A. Aransazo, Jr., A.C. No. 9701, February 10, 2021 — Hernando, J.; respondent suspended from the practice of law for one year.

Application: General reputational discomfort is not a license for a broad public disclosure, particularly when no claim requires a defense.

Conclusion: The lawyer must respond without revealing protected information.
CPRA, Canon II, Sections 40-41; Canon III, Sections 27-28.
Confidentiality exceptions are construed and used narrowly; a lawyer cannot manufacture one through public controversy.
Atty. Rogelio S. Constantino v. Atty. Nemesio A. Aransazo, Jr.
A.C. No. 9701, February 10, 2021 — Hernando, J.; respondent suspended from the practice of law for one year.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD201 • Final • Percentage fee shared with nonlawyer
A lawyer promises a nonlawyer claims agent thirty percent of every legal fee from clients the agent refers; is the agreement valid?

Answer: No. The arrangement shares legal fees with an unlicensed person and pays for client procurement.

Legal Basis: Canon III, Section 43 prohibits fee sharing with nonlawyers except a specific recognized exception; Canon II, Section 17 bars improper solicitation. The directly relevant authority is Tan Tek Beng v. Timoteo A. David, A.C. No. 1261, December 29, 1983 — Aquino, J.; fee-sharing and referral arrangement declared void and respondent reprimanded.

Application: The agent performs no legal service and is rewarded according to fees generated by referrals.

Conclusion: The agreement is void and professionally improper.
CPRA, Canon II, Section 17; Canon III, Section 43.
Fee-sharing and solicitation rules protect independent judgment and prevent commercialization of client procurement.
Tan Tek Beng v. Timoteo A. David
A.C. No. 1261, December 29, 1983 — Aquino, J.; fee-sharing and referral arrangement declared void and respondent reprimanded.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD201 • Final • Per-client referral bounty
A lawyer pays a hospital employee ₱5,000 for each accident victim who signs a retainer; does a fixed bounty avoid the fee-sharing rule?

Answer: No. Even if not expressed as a percentage, payment tied to procuring each client is improper solicitation and nonlawyer compensation for legal business.

Legal Basis: The CPRA looks to the transaction's purpose and effect, not only its arithmetic form. The directly relevant authority is Tan Tek Beng v. Timoteo A. David, A.C. No. 1261, December 29, 1983 — Aquino, J.; fee-sharing and referral arrangement declared void and respondent reprimanded.

Application: The hospital employee's reward depends on steering vulnerable prospective clients to the lawyer.

Conclusion: The bounty arrangement is prohibited.
CPRA, Canon II, Section 17; Canon III, Section 43.
A lawyer may not purchase clients through direct or indirect nonlawyer intermediaries.
Tan Tek Beng v. Timoteo A. David
A.C. No. 1261, December 29, 1983 — Aquino, J.; fee-sharing and referral arrangement declared void and respondent reprimanded.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD201 • Final • Ordinary staff salary versus fee sharing
A law office pays a nonlawyer receptionist a fixed market salary unrelated to cases obtained or fees collected; is that automatically prohibited fee sharing?

Answer: No. Ordinary compensation for legitimate nonlegal employment is not fee sharing when it is not contingent on legal fees or client procurement.

Legal Basis: Section 43 targets transfer of legal-fee interests to unlicensed persons, subject to its text and recognized exceptions. The directly relevant authority is Tan Tek Beng v. Timoteo A. David, A.C. No. 1261, December 29, 1983 — Aquino, J.; fee-sharing and referral arrangement declared void and respondent reprimanded.

Application: The receptionist is paid for administrative work at a fixed rate and has no percentage or referral stake.

Conclusion: The salary is permissible on the stated facts.
CPRA, Canon III, Section 43.
Substance distinguishes lawful staff compensation from a disguised share in legal fees or bounty for referrals.
Tan Tek Beng v. Timoteo A. David
A.C. No. 1261, December 29, 1983 — Aquino, J.; fee-sharing and referral arrangement declared void and respondent reprimanded.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD201 • Final • Association used to solicit clients

A lawyer forms a nonlawyer 'victims association' that cold-calls accident victims and forwards every signed client in exchange for half the attorney's fee; may the corporate form cure the arrangement?

Answer: No. A nonlawyer organization cannot be used to accomplish indirectly what the lawyer may not do directly.

Legal Basis: Sections 17 and 43 reach indirect solicitation and fee sharing. The directly relevant authority is Tan Tek Beng v. Timoteo A. David, A.C. No. 1261, December 29, 1983 — Aquino, J.; fee-sharing and referral arrangement declared void and respondent reprimanded.

Application: The association is a client-procurement mechanism financed by legal fees, not an independent public-service organization.

Conclusion: The scheme is prohibited.

Ethics rules follow beneficial ownership and practical function rather than labels or intermediaries.
Tan Tek Beng v. Timoteo A. David
A.C. No. 1261, December 29, 1983 — Aquino, J.; fee-sharing and referral arrangement declared void and respondent reprimanded.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD201 • Final • Gift tied to a referral
After every referred client pays, counsel sends the nonlawyer referrer an expensive 'thank-you gift' whose value tracks the fee; may counsel call it voluntary generosity?

Answer: No. A recurring benefit tied to referrals and fee amount is substance-wise compensation for procuring legal business.

Legal Basis: Improper solicitation and fee-sharing rules cannot be avoided by calling consideration a gift. The directly relevant authority is Tan Tek Beng v. Timoteo A. David, A.C. No. 1261, December 29, 1983 — Aquino, J.; fee-sharing and referral arrangement declared void and respondent reprimanded.

Application: Timing, repetition, and proportional value show a referral bargain rather than detached gratitude.

Conclusion: Counsel must stop the practice.
CPRA, Canon II, Section 17; Canon III, Section 43.
Professional regulation examines economic reality and prohibits disguised referral compensation.
Tan Tek Beng v. Timoteo A. David
A.C. No. 1261, December 29, 1983 — Aquino, J.; fee-sharing and referral arrangement declared void and respondent reprimanded.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD201 • Final • Practice of law beyond court appearances
A government lawyer spends twelve years drafting regulations, negotiating contracts, issuing legal opinions, and appearing before agencies but rarely enters a courtroom; has the lawyer practiced law?

Answer: Yes. Practice of law is not confined to litigation and includes habitual professional work requiring legal knowledge, training, and judgment.

Legal Basis: Cayetano v. Monsod sustained a broad, functional understanding of practice. The directly relevant authority is Renato L. Cayetano v. Christian Monsod, Hon. Jovito R. Salonga, Commission on Appointments, and Hon. Guillermo Carague, in his capacity as Secretary of Budget and Management, G.R. No. 100113, September 3, 1991 — Paras, J., En Banc; petition dismissed and Monsod's qualification sustained.

Application: The work applies law to rights, duties, public regulation, and representation on a continuing professional basis.

Conclusion: The experience qualifies as practice of law.
1987 Constitution, Article IX-C, Section 1(1); CPRA, Canon III, Section 1; Rules of Court, Rule 138, Section 1.
Practice of law includes advocacy, counseling, transactional work, and qualifying public service, not courtroom appearance alone.
Renato L. Cayetano v. Christian Monsod, Hon. Jovito R. Salonga, Commission on Appointments, and Hon. Guillermo Carague, in his capacity as Secretary of Budget and Management

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD201 • Final • Habitual legal counseling by a nonlawyer
A nonlawyer charges businesses monthly fees to interpret statutes, draft legal opinions, and negotiate their legal claims; is the service outside law practice because no court appearance occurs?

Answer: No. The recurring compensated work requires professional legal judgment and constitutes practice reserved to persons authorized by law.

Legal Basis: Rule 138 and the functional definition in Cayetano govern. The directly relevant authority is Renato L. Cayetano v. Christian Monsod, Hon. Jovito R. Conclusion: The nonlawyer may not render the service as described.

Unauthorized practice is determined by the nature of the legal work, not by the absence of courtroom advocacy.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD201 • Final • Self-representation and practice of law
A nonlawyer prepares and files one pleading solely for the nonlawyer's own case; does that isolated self-representation automatically make the person a practicing lawyer?

Answer: No. A party may appear personally where the rules allow, and isolated self-representation is not professional service rendered for another.

Legal Basis: Practice of law ordinarily involves authorized professional activity for clients or in a qualifying legal role. The directly relevant authority is Renato L. Cayetano v. Christian Monsod, Hon. Jovito R. Salonga, Commission on Appointments, and Hon. Guillermo Carague, in his capacity as Secretary of Budget and Management, G.R. No. 100113, September 3, 1991 — Paras, J., En Banc; petition dismissed and Monsod's qualification sustained.

Application: The person neither holds out as counsel nor serves another's legal interests.

Conclusion: The act is personal appearance, not proof of authorized law practice.
CPRA, Canon III, Section 1; Rules of Court, Rule 138, Section 1.
The right of a party to act personally is distinct from authority to practice law for others.
Renato L. Cayetano v. Christian Monsod, Hon. Jovito R. Salonga, Commission on Appointments, and Hon. Guillermo Carague, in his capacity as Secretary of Budget and Management

Does teaching law automatically satisfy every statutory requirement of active law practice?

Answer: Not automatically. Teaching may involve substantial legal scholarship and judgment, but the particular statute's text, the nature and continuity of work, and the candidate's actual professional functions must be examined.

Legal Basis: Cayetano adopts a broad functional approach rather than a single occupational label. The directly relevant authority is Renato L. Cayetano v. Christian Monsod, Hon. Jovito R. Application: A full-time professor who continuously analyzes law may present qualifying experience, but a one-time lecture does not establish the required period of practice.

Conclusion: Qualification requires evidence of sustained work fitting the governing functional standard.
CPRA, Canon III, Section 1; Rules of Court, Rule 138, Section 1.
Broad construction of law practice does not eliminate proof of duration, professional character, and statutory context.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD201 • Final • Friendship and appearance of partiality
A judge's close friend is a party in a pending case, and the judge publicly posts a photograph calling the party 'family'; must the judge address possible inhibition?

Answer: Yes. Friendship is not always an automatic ground, but these circumstances create a serious appearance question requiring disclosure and assessment under the current inhibition framework.

Legal Basis: The reasonable, fair-minded, informed observer standard governs appearance of impartiality. The directly relevant authority is Re: Letter of Presiding Justice Conrado M. Reyes reprimanded, and Vidal admonished; motions for reconsideration denied with finality October 15, 2008.

Application: Publicly proclaimed closeness while the case is pending may cause reasonable doubt even without proof that merits were discussed.

Conclusion: The judge must disclose the relationship and inhibit if impartiality may reasonably be questioned.
2025 CJCA, Canon III, Sections 2, 4, 6, and 12; Canon IV, Section 7.
Judicial ethics protects both actual neutrality and public confidence in neutral process.

A litigant privately messages the judge about the strength of evidence while the case is pending, and the judge replies, 'I understand'; is the exchange proper?

Answer: No. The communication concerns an issue in a pending case outside the official proceeding and without the other party.

Application: Even a short response risks encouraging private access and undermining appearance of impartiality.

Conclusion: The judge should end, preserve, and disclose or otherwise address the contact under applicable procedure.
2025 CJCA, Canon III, Sections 2, 5, and 6.
Digital convenience does not relax the prohibition on one-sided communications about pending matters.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD201 • Final • Disclosure and agreement after a nonmandatory concern
A judge discloses a remote past professional association that may affect appearance but is not a mandatory disqualification ground; may the judge continue if all parties agree?

Answer: Yes, when the current Code permits continuation after full disclosure and the parties' agreement, provided the judge remains able to act impartially and the agreement is embodied in an order.

Legal Basis: Canon III, Section 12 supplies the disclosure-and-agreement mechanism for appropriate circumstances. The directly relevant authority is Re: Letter of Presiding Justice Conrado M. Vasquez, Jr. on CA-G.R. SP No. 103692 [Antonio Rosete, et al. v. Securities and Exchange Commission, et al.], A.M. No. 08-8-11-CA, September 9, 2008 — Per Curiam, En Banc; Roxas dismissed, Sabio suspended for two months, Vasquez severely reprimanded, B.L. Reyes reprimanded, and Vidal admonished; motions for reconsideration denied with finality October 15, 2008.

Application: The association is remote, no current interest exists, and the parties knowingly agree after disclosure.

Conclusion: The judge may continue through the prescribed written process.
2025 CJCA, Canon III, Sections 2, 6, and 12.
Remittal of a nonmandatory concern requires transparency, informed agreement, and preserved actual impartiality.
Re: Letter of Presiding Justice Conrado M. Vasquez, Jr. on CA-G.R. SP No. 103692 [Antonio Rosete, et al. v. Securities and Exchange Commission, et al.]

Basic Legal and Judicial Ethics
LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD201 • Final • Reasoned order of inhibition
May a judge issue a one-word order stating only 'Inhibited' without identifying any reason or furnishing the offices required by the current Code?

Answer: No. Every inhibition order must state the reason and be furnished to the parties and the designated judicial offices.

Legal Basis: Canon III, Section 13 creates transparency and administrative-accountability requirements. The directly relevant authority is Re: Letter of Presiding Justice Conrado M. Vasquez, Jr. on CA-G.R. SP No. 103692 [Antonio Rosete, et al. v. Securities and Exchange Commission, et al.], A.M. No. 08-8-11-CA, September 9, 2008 — Per Curiam, En Banc; Roxas dismissed, Sabio suspended for two months, Vasquez severely reprimanded, B.L. Reyes reprimanded, and Vidal admonished; motions for reconsideration denied with finality October 15, 2008.

Application: A bare conclusion prevents review of whether recusal was principled and complicates reassignment and case management.

Conclusion: The judge must issue a compliant reasoned order.
2025 CJCA, Canon III, Section 13.
Inhibition is a judicial act requiring stated grounds, not an unexplained personal option.

Basic Legal and Judicial Ethics
LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD201 • Final • Inappropriate association with counsel
During trial, the judge repeatedly travels socially with one side's lawyer and appears in promotional posts describing their special access; no case discussion is proved; is there an ethics concern?

Answer: Yes. Conduct can undermine impartiality by appearance even without proof of an express bargain or case discussion.

Legal Basis: The 2025 CJCA prohibits interaction or association tending to compromise, or appear to compromise, impartiality. The directly relevant authority is Re: Letter of Presiding Justice Conrado M. Vasquez, Jr. on CA-G.R. SP No. 103692 [Antonio Rosete, et al. v. Securities and Exchange Commission, et al.], A.M. No. 08-8-11-CA, September 9, 2008 — Per Curiam, En Banc; Roxas dismissed, Sabio suspended for two months, Vasquez severely reprimanded, B.L. Reyes reprimanded, and Vidal admonished; motions for reconsideration denied with finality October 15, 2008.

Application: Repeated public displays of special access during trial would concern a reasonable informed observer and suggest preferential treatment.

Conclusion: The judge must disclose, consider inhibition, and cease inappropriate association.
2025 CJCA, Canon III, Sections 2-4 and 6.
The appearance standard addresses relationships that erode confidence before actual bias can be proved.

Basic Legal and Judicial Ethics
LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD201 • Final • Private belief and adjudication
May a judge decide cases through private supernatural consultations and announce that the consultations override the evidence?

Answer: No. A judge may hold private beliefs, but those beliefs may not dictate adjudication, replace law and evidence, or be imposed on court users.

Legal Basis: Canon VI requires competent, personal decision-making, and Canon IV protects freedom of belief only within the limits of impartial lawful judging. The directly relevant authority is Office of the Court Administrator v. Judge Florentino V. Floro, Jr.; Re: Resolution Dated 11 May 1999 of Judge Florentino V. Floro, Jr.; Luz Arriego v. Judge Florentino V. Floro, Jr., A.M. No. RTJ-99-1460; A.M. No. 99-7-273-RTC; A.M. No. RTJ-06-1988, March 31, 2006 — Chico-Nazario, J., En Banc; ₱40,000 fine on seven charges, nonpenal medical separation with three years' back salaries, RTJ-06-1988 dismissed, and 99-7-273-RTC dismissed as moot.

Application: The judge has displaced the record and legal judgment with an unverifiable private source.

Conclusion: The conduct is ethically incompatible with judicial office.
2025 CJCA, Canon IV, Section 13(c)-(d); Canon VI, Sections 1 and 3.
Discipline addresses misuse of belief in official decision-making, not belief itself.
